localChanges: When one of your Wonders becomes obsolete, a button appears beside End Turn rather than a window you have to close. Click it to read the news and jump to the city. It never holds up the end of the turn, and goes once you end a turn yourself, so a string of automatic turns can't clear it before you've seen it.

When a civilization is defeated or adds to its spaceship, the alert now only names it if you have met it — through a negotiation or declaration, or by having seen one of its cities. Otherwise it reads "an unknown civilization" (#59).
When one of your Wonders becomes obsolete, you are now told, once (#60).

Clicking the empty space beyond a pole no longer selects a tile from the far side of the world. A hard drag or flick stops at the pole instead of jumping to the other one. Nothing drawn on the last row, such as a city's name, spills over the first.
Options now has a map scale, from 1× to 4×, which takes effect straight away and keeps the same spot in the middle of the screen.
A new "Stop the map at the poles" option keeps the view from scrolling past the top or bottom of the world, on the map and on the minimap alike (#13).
Only the first finger pans the map. Touching or lifting another no longer stops a glide, ends the drag or counts as a tap on the tile under it.

Press and drag anywhere on the map to pan it; let go mid-drag and it glides to a stop, and pressing again catches it. A quick click still centres on a tile or opens a city or unit, and a long press still opens the unit's actions.
Selecting a unit near the edge of the map now brings it back to the middle, rather than waiting until it is off-screen. How close counts as "near" is a new setting under Options (#14).

Pressing F5 during a game opened the Trade Report and, on top of it, a box asking whether you wanted to reload the page. It just opens the Trade Report now. F5 on the main menu, and Ctrl+R (Cmd+R on a Mac) at any time, still check before reloading (#10).

W (wait) is meant to put a unit to one side and come back to it once everything else has moved, but it only ever flicked to the next unit, and the one you skipped could turn straight back up. A unit you wait now goes to the back of the queue and returns after every other unit has had its turn, longest-waiting first. Waiting your last unit simply keeps it selected (#10).

F5 was handled by two keydown listeners: the reload guard (fires everywhere) and the leader-screens map (fires once a game is running, opening TradeReport), so in-game F5 showed both. The reload guard now only claims F5 before a game starts; Ctrl/Cmd+R still always confirms a reload (#10).

W was mapped to a non-existent 'Wait' unit action, so it always fell through to a plain cycle to the next active unit, and the unit was never deferred. W now sends the current unit to the back of a queue: waited units (tracked by id, since every update reconstitutes fresh objects) are held out of auto-selection until every other active unit has had its turn, then come back longest-waiting first. When everything else is already waiting, W wraps round to the longest-waiting unit; with a single active unit it keeps that unit selected (#10).

The map used to hold a full-size copy of the whole world for every layer it draws — seven of them, over a hundred and thirty megabytes before a single tile appears, and more again on a bigger map. Each layer is now only as big as the window you are looking through, which hands back about ninety-five megabytes and stops the cost growing with the map (#7).

It redraws only the part of the screen that actually changed, too. Scrolling moves the picture it already has and fills in the strip coming into view, and the unit waiting for orders blinks by repainting its own tile instead of the entire map.
Resizing the window could leave the map blank until something else happened to redraw it. It comes straight back now.

Every layer was a canvas the size of the whole world — 2560x1920 at 80x60 scale 2, and seven of them, 137.4 MB before a tile is drawn, growing with the map. A layer is now the size of the portal that composites it, with `#originX` and `#originY` saying which world pixel sits at its top left corner: 40.0 MB for the same world, and a world twice the size costs the same again.

That means a tile no longer has one fixed place on a canvas, and because the world wraps it can have several places or none. Layers are handed the places to draw in rather than working them out from the tile's co-ordinates — `drawTile(tile, offsetX, offsetY)`, called once per place — so `Portal` has no wrap offsets to composite any more, and the overflow `CityNames` used to draw a canvas-width away to survive being tiled is now just another placement. Moving the view blits the overlap across and draws only the strips it uncovers.

Layers record what they changed, and `Portal.render()` composites those regions rather than the whole canvas, which is what restricting the blink tick to the active unit's region needed: `ActiveUnit` is the topmost layer, so un-drawing it means restoring the pixels beneath it. A blink composite is 0.006 megapixels and 5.5 `drawImage` calls against 10.5 and 7 for a full one. Regions are unioned until none overlap, because compositing a pixel twice doubles up anything drawn with alpha, and past half the canvas or eight regions it composites the lot instead. What a tile draws past its own square is recorded as it is drawn rather than declared per layer, so the city glyph, a yield icon and the copy behind a stack all reach the composite without the sprite sizes being second-guessed.

Verified in the browser on an 80x60 world at scale 2 in a 1712x873 portal: after panning, city windows, overlay toggles and blinks the incrementally composited portal is pixel-identical to a full composite, and a viewport reached by short scrolling hops is pixel-identical to the same viewport drawn from nothing — 0 of 1,494,576 pixels differ in each case. The geometry underneath is exhaustively tested offline.

Fixed on the way: the resize handler assigned `mapPortal.width` and `height` unconditionally, and assigning either clears a canvas even when the value has not changed. A resize that resized nothing therefore wiped the map, and with the portal compositing only what changed it put nothing back.

The map used to build its scenery on six separate world-sized canvases and stack them up on every redraw, then composite every one of them at every wrapped position — including positions entirely off the screen. It draws the same picture from one canvas now, and only over the part of the screen it actually covers: sixty draws and nearly three hundred megapixels a frame down to fifteen and seven and a half, and about ninety megabytes of memory handed back (#7).

The minimap turned out to be the more expensive half, once the map stopped drowning it out. It made its picture by shrinking three full-size copies of the world down to a couple of hundred pixels across, every time anything changed. It has a small picture of its own now, drawn at the size it is actually shown: terrain in flat colours, cities in their owner's colour so you can see whose land is whose, and nothing at all where you have not been yet (#53).

The unit waiting for orders shows there as a flashing white tile, so you can find it at a glance and click straight to it. Clicking takes you where you clicked, too — it used to land two tiles up and to the left (#54).

The minimap is drawn at a whole number of pixels per tile and scaled up, rather than squeezed down to a fractional size, so it is sharp for the first time. And the box showing the part of the world you are looking at comes back round the other side when the map wraps, instead of running off the edge and leaving half of itself behind.

`Minimap.update()` composited by scaling three full-world canvases down to 190px wide — 14.7 megapixels thrown away on every patch and every recentre. Over 15s of stress play that was 383.4 megapixels against the portal's 310.9, so the minimap had quietly become the larger consumer of the two. It draws from an `Overview` layer rendered at a few pixels a tile now: 0.79 megapixels over the same window, and one blit an update rather than three. A tile change repaints one tile instead of the world.

The overview draws terrain as one flat colour per type, cities in the owner's colour so rival territory can be read at a glance, and nothing at all for unexplored, so how much of the world is still dark stays legible. Terrains come from a registry plugins extend, so anything the colour table does not know falls back to land or water rather than leaving a hole. It deliberately ignores the layers' `isVisible()`: hiding yields or units is a view mode for the map, not for an overview.

The active unit is a white tile that flashes in time with the main map, so it can be found on the minimap and clicked to centre without reaching for the keyboard. Flashing means redrawing the minimap twice a second, which is only affordable now the layer is small.
The minimap is rendered at a whole number of pixels a tile and upscaled by CSS rather than drawn at a fractional size, so the tiles are finally crisp.

Clicking it now centres where you clicked. `event.offsetX` is already relative to the canvas but the handler subtracted the element's `offsetLeft` as well, and `Math.ceil` should have been `Math.floor`, which together landed the map two tiles up and left of the click.

The world wraps but the box showing what the portal is looking at did not, so centring near an edge drew it running off that side with nothing coming back on the opposite one — a viewport that was plainly half missing. `rawVisibleRange()` is unwrapped by design, so the box is now drawn from its wrapped origin and again a world earlier on whichever axis overflows. The copies' outer edges fall off the canvas, so the two halves meet without a seam. This was the `TODO: draw the rectangle replicated when close to the sides` that sat on the old rect.
Both edges are floored now rather than the width being floored on its own, so a box covers the same tiles however it is split.

Scoping the viewport-buffer work turned up that `Minimap.update()` is the renderer's largest source-pixel consumer: it discards 14.7 megapixels into a 190x142 target on every patch and every recentre, 383.4 megapixels over 15s of stress play against the portal's 310.9. It is also the whole of the blocker on viewport-sized buffers, being the only thing outside `Portal` that reads a layer's `canvas()`. Filed as #53 with the decisions on what a dedicated minimap layer draws, and #54 for the click landing two tiles up and left of the tile clicked.

The six layers that draw a tile's own scenery — land and coast, irrigation, terrain, improvements, terrain features and goody huts — were six world-sized canvases the portal composited in order on every render. Nothing ever toggled any of them on its own and they only change when a tile changes, so they are one `Landscape` canvas now, drawn in the same order. The main portal holds seven world canvases instead of twelve, and the city portal six instead of ten; the city map gains goody huts, which it had been the only portal not to draw.

`Portal.render()` drew every layer at every wrapped offset as a full-layer blit, including offsets that fell entirely off the canvas. It works out once, for all the layers, which repeats land on the canvas and which part of each one does. On an 80x60 world at scale 2 in a 1712x873 portal that takes a render from 60.5 `drawImage` calls and 297 megapixels of source down to 15.0 calls and 7.5 megapixels.
The marker for a road with no neighbouring road called `rect()` and `fill()` without a `beginPath()`, so every marker re-filled every isolated road drawn before it. It begins a path now.
Importing SP257.PIC and TER257.PIC used to lock the page up for well over two minutes. It now finishes in about a quarter of a second, and the page stays responsive while it does (#50).

The work was one loop: knocking the transparent colour out of each sprite read the canvas a single pixel at a time, and swept the whole 320x200 source image rather than the sprite sitting in the corner of it — eighteen million reads to handle sixty-nine thousand pixels. The extracted sprites are unchanged, right down to the pixel. Writing them to the browser's database is one transaction now rather than one per sprite, and the dialog no longer warns you to go and make a cup of tea.

`pnpm update @civ-clone/civ1-asset-extractor` repoints the lockfile from ee19340 to 4860507, which is the per-sprite `getImageData` rewrite the previous commit measured. The renderer consumed the extractor straight from its default branch, so the import stayed slow until the lockfile moved.

log: The transparency pass called `getImageData(x, y, 1, 1)` once per pixel, and looped over the 320x200 source canvas rather than the sprite's own bounds, so ~99.6% of the iterations read outside the sprite and did nothing. Across the 286 sprites in `extract-data.json` that is 18,304,002 readbacks to process 69,194 pixels.

One `getImageData` over the sprite, a walk of the buffer zeroing matching pixels, and one `putImageData` does the same job in 288 readbacks. Verified pixel-identical output for all 286 sprites from `TER257.PIC` and `SP257.PIC`.
Refs civ-clone/web-renderer#50.

localChanges: Refs #50. The bulk of the cost was in `civ1-asset-extractor`, where the transparency pass called `getImageData(x, y, 1, 1)` once per pixel and looped over the 320x200 source canvas rather than the sprite's own bounds — 18,304,002 readbacks to process 69,194 pixels. Fixed there (civ-clone/civ1-asset-extractor@4860507) as one `getImageData` per sprite, and verified pixel-identical for all 286.

The remaining two items are here. `ImportAssetsWindow` wrote with `Promise.all(results.map((record) => assetStore.set(record)))`, and `Store.set` opens its own transaction, so 286 assets meant 286 transactions; `Store.setAll` puts them all in one. `assetStore.keys()` was also fetched once per input file from inside the per-file loop, and is now fetched once up front.

Measured in Chrome against `SP257.PIC` + `TER257.PIC` with "replace existing" on: 144,740ms before, 268ms after — 144,138ms of extraction becomes 76ms, and 602ms of writing becomes 28ms. The page no longer freezes for the duration, so the worker in item 4 of the issue is not needed; the dialog's "can take at least a few minutes" now says it takes a moment. A fresh import writes all 286 assets and a new game renders them with the transparency intact.

Eleven of the entries in this window were blank, including one for every release: a commit written as a subject with no body had that subject mistaken for a `Co-Authored-By:`-style trailer and thrown away. They have their text back, and an entry with nothing in it is no longer shown at all.
The end-of-turn button now dims and stops responding the moment it is pressed, rather than sitting there inviting a second press that would send the turn twice.

Closes #11. `activate()` set `disabled` on `element()`, which is the wrapping `.action` div, and the attribute means nothing on a div: the button neither disabled nor dimmed, and both the click handler and the keyboard handler in `Actions` would call `activate()` again and send a second `EndTurn` to the engine.

It now disables the `button` itself and returns early when it is already disabled, so the turn ends once. `.action button:disabled` dims it and stops the end-of-turn glow, and the next turn's actions arrive as a freshly built `EndTurn`, so it comes back enabled on its own.

Verified in the browser: on press the button reports `disabled`, `grayscale(0.7) brightness(0.6)` and no `::before` animation, and the next turn's panel has an enabled one again. The `img` tag in `build()` was also missing its closing `>`.

Closes #51. `toBullets` tested every line of a single-paragraph message against `TRAILER`, and `/^[A-Za-z][\w-]*: \S/` matches `release: …` and `docs: …` exactly as it matches `Co-Authored-By: …`. A commit with a subject and nothing else therefore had its only line thrown away, and eleven of the 159 entries in `releases.json` rendered as an empty block. Eight were `release:` commits, so every release was contributing an empty block to the one after it.

A trailer is only a trailer below the first line. The filter now starts at the second, the eleven entries have been backfilled with the subjects they lost, and `ReleaseWindow` skips an entry with no local and no external changes so nothing empty can reach the window whatever the cause.

`npm run test:changelog` covers the message shapes and asserts no entry in `releases.json` is empty; it fails on each of the three shapes the old filter dropped. The module guard also no longer throws when the file is imported with no `process.argv[1]`, as `node -e` does.

A city on the first or last column had its name cut in half, and a city on the bottom row had no name at all: the label is drawn centred on the city and wider than the tile, and whatever hung past the edge of the map was thrown away rather than continuing round the other side. It now continues round.

Selecting a unit, or moving one, used to redraw every unit on the map -- over twelve hundred tiles for a single step -- when only two tiles can have changed: the one the unit left and the one it arrived at. City names were being redrawn the same way, wiping the whole layer and searching the entire world for cities on every message from the game. Between them they were the last two places the renderer still did a full-map pass, so nothing does one now.
docs: record the CityNames work and tick off the zero-width image crash

The label is centred on its tile and wider than it, so at the edges of the layer canvas the overhang was clipped and, because that canvas is what the portal tiles, appeared nowhere at all (#49). On an 80x50 world at scale 2, `uMgungundlovu` on the first or last column lost 46 of its 124 pixels, and any name on the last row was drawn entirely below the canvas and was invisible.

`World.get` wraps both axes and `Portal.render()` tiles the canvas on both, so a label crossing an edge is now drawn a second time offset by the canvas width or height, which puts the overflow where the adjacent tiled copy shows it.

`4607766` set out to fix the last-row case by taking `(x * size) % canvas.width` for the offsets. That is a no-op — `x` is always below the world width, so the product is always below the canvas width — and the case was still broken.

While in here, `update()` now honours the tiles it is passed. It used to ignore them, clear the whole canvas and walk every tile in the world looking for cities, on every patch (#48). It keeps track of where each label was drawn instead, so it can clear just the boxes an update invalidated and redraw only the labels that overlapped them — a label overhangs its neighbours, so clearing one can bite into another. Measured over comparable windows of automated play, the layer went from seventeen full-canvas clears (4,915,200 pixels each) to 245,160 pixels cleared in total, and is now the least of the twelve layers rather than the only one clearing everything.

Verified in the browser against a real asset import: `Ulaanbaatar` and its size digit render correctly, no layer performs a full-canvas clear any more, and the wrap was confirmed by replicating the geometry and text metrics exactly — pixels now land at both edges for the first and last columns, and at the top for the last row, where before there were none.
docs: record the Units layer fix and the CityNames full-world rescan

`renderActiveUnit` re-rendered the entire `Units` layer on every unit selection and every unit move: a full-canvas clear plus a `renderTile` for every tile in the world, measured at 1,207 per-tile clears for a single unit move (#47).

It now redraws only the tiles that an active-unit change actually invalidates. `Units` skips whichever tile holds the active unit, so exactly two tiles go stale: the one being vacated, which has to draw its unit again, and the one taking over, which has to stop drawing it. Everything else reaches this layer the way it reaches the other eleven, through `portal.build(tilesToRender)`.

The tiles are collected in `applyActiveUnit`, which is the only point that still knows the outgoing unit. The `update([lastUnit.tile, unit.tile])` that used to follow the full render could not do this job: `applyActiveUnit` has already pointed `lastUnit` at the incoming unit by the time the coalesced render runs, so that call was passing the same tile twice and never touching the tile the unit came from. The full render was doing the real work, which is why dropping it on its own -- as the issue proposed -- would have left the previous unit missing from the layer.

Verified in the browser against a real asset import: cycling the active unit with `w` leaves every other unit drawn, stacked units still render, a 128-turn automated soak shows no vanished or duplicated sprites, and no layer performs a full-canvas clear any more except `CityNames`, which clears and rescans the world on every patch for its own reasons.

Opening a city could throw before it drew anything, the first time a unit's picture was needed: the picture was measured before the browser had finished loading it, so it measured as nothing at all. Everything that draws from the imported artwork now waits for it, and the pictures it builds from it -- a unit in its civilization's colours, a stretch of coastline, a scaled icon -- are kept and reused instead of being rebuilt for every frame.

The torch cursor appears for the first time as a result. It had never worked: it was the first thing to ask for a scaled picture, so it always asked too early, and the blank it got back was then kept and handed out for the rest of the session.

The map also leaves itself alone when there is nothing to animate, rather than recompositing all eleven layers twice a second to blink a unit that is not there, and the blinking unit's layer is erased a tile at a time instead of wholesale.
The tick only flipped the active-unit layer's visibility; it never re-rendered it, so the full-canvas clear was per activate/move rather than twice a second.

The 500 ms tick toggled the active-unit layer and composited all eleven visible layers unconditionally. With no active unit that layer draws nothing, so the toggle was invisible and the composite was pure waste twice a second (#45). It now skips both, and still drains any pending tiles and composites when it had tiles to build. `renderActiveUnit` sets the layer visible again whenever a unit becomes active, so leaving the flag untouched is safe.

`ActiveUnit.render()` also inherited `Map.clear()`, wiping the entire layer canvas -- 2560x1920 here -- to draw one 32px tile. It now clears only the region it last drew, which measures as a single 34x34 clear (tile plus the stacked-unit offset) where there was previously a full-canvas one.

Verified in the browser against a real asset import: the blink still runs at exactly one composite per 500 ms while a unit is active, the unit's terrain is cleanly restored on each off-phase, and moving the active unit leaves no trail at the tiles it came from.
docs: mark the render hot-path caching item done

`AssetStore.getImage` created a detached ``, set `src`, and returned it without waiting. A detached element is never rendered, so its intrinsic size is 0 until it loads -- and `scaleImage` sized its canvas from `image.width`. The result was a 0x0 canvas, which `getScaled` then cached permanently under that path, so any icon that lost the race stayed blank for the rest of the session and `toDataURL()` handed consumers `"data:,"`.

The torch cursor was the reliable casualty: it is the first `getScaled` call in `Renderer.init`, so it always lost, and `document.body.style.cursor` silently fell back to `default`. It now resolves to a real 26x26 image.

`getImage` waits for the `load` event before caching, and leaves a failed image uncached so a later import can replace it. Deliberately not `decode()`: for an element that is not in the document, `decode()` never settles while the page is hidden, and this is awaited during init, so it stopped the app starting at all in a background tab.
`scaleImage` sizes from `imageSize` and returns a 1x1 rather than a default-sized canvas for a source with no dimensions, which consumers would otherwise embed as a visibly empty 300x150 box.
`getScaled` keys on the scale as well as the path. Keying on the path alone served the first scale asked for to every later caller; every call site uses 2 today, so this was latent.

Same root cause as the clone in `getPreloadedImage` (#8): an image measured before it has loaded. Verified with a real asset import -- init reliable over four consecutive loads with the document hidden, the cursor correct, and the City details report's scaled yield icons all rendering at 14x14 with none blank.

`getPreloadedImage` returned `image.cloneNode()` on every lookup. A clone is detached, so it is neither rendered nor decoded and its `width` reads 0 on first use -- which `replaceColours` fed straight into `getImageData` as a zero-sized rect, throwing `IndexSizeError` the first time a unit image was used (the city build header) (#8). No caller mutated the element, so the clone was also an allocation per lookup on the render hot path.

Return the preloaded element itself and size from `naturalWidth`/ `naturalHeight`, which the `#preload` originals report correctly because the container clips them rather than hiding them. `replaceColours` and `Map.putImage` now bail out on a source with no dimensions instead of throwing, since the preload is asynchronous and an early render can arrive first.
With the clone gone the derived canvases can be cached rather than rebuilt:
`replaceColours` returns its cache entry directly instead of cloning it per hit, and keys on the source colours too -- the same sprite recoloured from a different source set is a different result.
`renderUnit` caches the fully rendered unit, keyed on type, colours, fortified and busy state, and composites the overlays onto its own canvas so it never draws on the shared recolour entry.
`Map/Land` caches the composed coast tile by its 8-neighbour bitmask, which bounds it at 256 small canvases instead of one per coast tile per render.
A cache entry is skipped whenever it would be built from an image that had not decoded, so a missing sprite cannot stick for the session, and all three drop when the preload container changes.

Verified against a real asset import (TER257.PIC/SP257.PIC) with the stress harness: 171 turns, no render errors, no zero-sized `getImageData`, and `getImageData` calls -- one per recolour cache miss -- flat at 6 to 12 across the run rather than one per unit per render.
Split the render hot-path items to match how they actually group:
The image/canvas cloning item (#6) absorbs the zero-width getImageData crash (#8) -- both come from getPreloadedImage returning a detached cloneNode(), which is neither rendered nor decoded.

The blink tick splits in two. Restricting it to the active unit's region needs a partial portal composite, because ActiveUnit is the topmost layer and un-drawing it means restoring the pixels beneath, so that half moves to the dirty-rect work (#7). The half that needs none of that machinery is #45.
Also fold the science-window turns count and the map edge lock into the existing entries for their tickets (#15, #13), rather than leaving them under the rendering heading.
release: a save from a game under way loads again

Loading a save made much past the opening turns did nothing at all: the page did not reload, and nothing was said. A save is handed to the reloading page through browser storage, and it was handed over as uncompressed JSON — 1.6MB on turn 1, but 7.7MB by turn 130 and 11.5MB on a turn-110 game with more of a world in it — against a `sessionStorage` limit of about 5MB. The write threw `QuotaExceededError` outside the `try` that reports a save it cannot read, so the failure was silent (#5).

The save goes through IndexedDB now, which has no such limit, and takes it whether or not the browser can compress. A marker is left in `sessionStorage`, which is what keeps a save waiting mid-reload belonging to the tab that is reloading rather than to every tab on the site, and means an ordinary page load never opens the database at all.
A hand-over that fails now says so, leaves nothing behind, and leaves the game you are playing where it is.
release: a destroyed city no longer keeps a worked tile
A destroyed city no longer keeps a worked tile (#4). Conformance unchanged, every gate green: 330 packages one copy each, 101 checkouts matching their installed copy, every suite passing.

log: Capturing a size 1 city shrinks it to nothing, and `shrink` destroys it, which releases its tiles. `reassign-workers` runs after `shrink`, though, and handed the dead city its centre back. It is checked inside the effect rather than as a `Criterion`: `RuleRegistry.process` validates every rule before running any effect, so a `Criterion` still sees the city as it was before `shrink`.

That leftover centre then does the damage. A city founded on the site takes the centre back and processes `TileReassigned` for the old city, and `assign-workers` gave it the best tile still free: a tile marked as worked by another city, which the new city could never work (civ-clone/web-renderer#4). `tile-reassigned/assign-workers` now skips a destroyed city.
Both have a test, and both tests fail without the change.

localChanges: `World.get(x, y)` copied all 2,400 tiles to index one of them, on every one of the eight neighbour lookups each tile makes. Counting the copies found 490 million tile references moved in thirty turns; it is 7.5 million now, and a 150-turn headless run takes 15.9s against 19.0s before.

core-registry@0.1.4, core-world@0.1.18 and core-game@0.1.5. 150 turns runs in 15.9s against the published artifacts, conformance unchanged, every gate green: 330 packages one copy each, 101 checkouts matching their installed copy, all six suites passing.

log: A transient field with no entry in `Game.inject` arrives as `undefined`, and `assertInjected` says so rather than letting a loaded game read it — which is how this was caught, by `tests/engine/inject.ts`, the moment `core-world` gained the field.
`() => null` because that is what the lazy guard in `World.get` is written against, the same as `_valueCache`.

`length` was `this.entries().length`, and `entries()` returns a defensive copy — so asking a registry how big it was copied every entry to read a number off the copy. A subclass that overrides `entries()` to reorder, as `RuleRegistry` does, has the same count either way.

`get(x, y)` was `this.entries()[coordsToIndex(x, y)]`, and `EntityRegistry.entries()` hands back a defensive copy — right for a caller that might sort or splice what it gets, ruinous for one that wants a single element. `Tile.getNeighbour` calls `get` eight times per tile, so counting the copies over thirty turns found 204,552 calls moving 490 million tile references: 98.5% of all registry copying in the run, on a 60x40 world of 2,400 tiles.

`_tileCache` holds the tiles in registration order, rebuilt lazily and dropped on `register`, which is the only way `_tiles` changes — nothing unregisters a tile from the world. `build` and `onHydrated` now go through `register` rather than reaching past it, so neither can leave a stale cache behind.
`entries()` still copies. It is public and callers do sort what they get; only `get` is served from the cache.
150 turns, measured back to back: 19.0 / 19.0 / 18.8s before, 16.1 / 16.4 / 16.4s after, with core-registry's `length`. Conformance checksums unchanged.

localChanges: `tools/registry-profile.js` counts `EntityRegistry.entries()` calls and copied elements per registry class, for the same reason `rule-profile.js` exists: a CPU profile attributes all of this to one frame and cannot say whose registry it is.

It contradicted #42's guess twice over. `RuleRegistry` was **59 calls** — the per-rule-type cache works, and re-sorting 924 rules was not happening. What it found instead was a plain `EntityRegistry` at 204,552 calls copying 490 million elements, 2,400 per call, which is exactly the tile count of a 60x40 world: `World.get(x, y)` copying every tile to index one of them.
98.5% of all registry copying in a thirty-turn run, now 7.5M elements down from 498M.
Refs #4. A tile in Tlaxcala's radius showed as worked by another city, and Tlaxcala could not work it. The save had a `WorkedTile` for Teotihuacan, destroyed years earlier on the same site.

The cause is in `civ1-city` and is fixed there (civ-clone/civ1-city@6c8f67c): capturing a size 1 city destroyed it and then gave it its centre back, and a city founded on the site later swapped that centre for the best tile left. Saves made before that fix still hold the tile, so `restoreGame` now releases any tile worked by a destroyed city right after hydrating.
`npm run test:worked-tiles` checks the release; the conformance game is unchanged with the `civ1-city` fix synced in, and every suite passes.
release: captured cities and other players' wonders name their city

Fixes #43. When another civilization finished a wonder in a city we had seen, "Wonder completed" read ` {{city}} } has completed work on Colossus!`. The string passed `"city": {{city}}` to `Generic.city-name`, which takes a name and a civilization, and the notification never sent a `city` at all. It now uses the city's name and founder like every other city string.

The notification sent `{ cityBuild, build }`, and `cityBuild` is the other player's build queue: the visibility filter doesn't wrap it, so its `available`, `building`, `cost`, `progress` and `remaining` all went across. It now sends the city, which goes as an `UnknownCity`, and the wonder. The variant for a city we have never seen sends only the wonder, since it was naming a city we aren't meant to know about.
`npm run test:translations` covers both variants; it fails on the old string.
Fixes #2. Losing Asansol to Babylon read "Babylon have captured our city `{{city.originalPlayer.civilization._}}.Asansol.name`!".

City names are looked up by the civilization that founded the city (`Generic.city-name` is given `city.originalPlayer`), but another player's city is sent as an `UnknownCity`, which carried only its current owner. By the time the notification is sent the city is Babylon's, so it went as an `UnknownCity` and the founder was missing. `UnknownCity` now carries `originalPlayer` as well — already public, since the name itself gives it away — and the other strings that name another player's city resolve the same way.
`City.captured-by-us` was already right in practice: the city is ours by then and sent in full.
`npm run test:translations` now serialises a notification with an `UnknownCity`, rebuilds it as the UI does and checks both captured messages; it fails without the change.
release: J. S. Bach's Cathedral keeps its name in the city build UI
Fixes #3. Two separate faults, both triggered by the apostrophe.

The "currently building" header read `J. S. Bach's Cathedral`. i18next HTML-escapes `{{item}}`, and the header sets the label as text, so the entity was shown literally. `City.Build.title`, `City.Build.build-item` and `City.CompleteProduction.body` now interpolate the name with `{{- item}}`.

The choose list showed only ` 400 / 80 turns)`. `CityBuildSelectionWindow` translates each label, then `SelectionWindow` passed the finished string through `t()` again, and i18next read the `:` in `(Cost: …` as a namespace separator. `SelectionWindow` now uses a given label as-is and only translates the value when there is no label (as `Revolution` relies on). Every other caller already passes translated labels. The options are built as elements with `textContent`, so names are no longer spliced into markup unescaped.
`npm run test:translations` checks the three keys against Bach's, Michelangelo's and Magellan's; it fails on the old strings.

`generate-changelog.mjs` writes `changelog/<sha>.json` for each commit it turns into an entry, alongside `changelog/releases.json`, and both are tracked — 2233b2e is the shape. Today's two release commits staged only `releases.json`, leaving five behind.
No effect on the site: `releases.json` is what the bundle imports, and it was committed and deployed correctly both times. These are the per-commit records the generator reads back.
release: tile distance without building all nine of them

core-world@0.1.17 and core-save-game@0.1.7. 150 turns runs in 20.7s against the published artifacts, conformance unchanged, every gate green: 330 packages one copy each, 101 checkouts matching their installed copy, all six suites passing.

log: `{ handler: () => {} }.handler` is not anonymous — the property key names it — so it used to be written as `{ $class: 'handler' }` and fail on load, in someone else's session, with "unknown entity type". The class check added for the `Gold` collision already closes it: a name has to resolve back to the very class it was read from, and `handler` resolves to nothing.

`save` passes the class registry on every entity, so this holds for real saves and not only for calls that opt in. Nothing was covering the named case; the existing test only covered a genuinely anonymous function.
Closes #19.

`distanceFrom` built every way two tiles could be separated across a wrapping world — three horizontal wraps times three vertical — called `Math.hypot` on each, sorted the nine results and returned the first. Per call that allocated nine pairs and nine results, sorted them, and discarded eight. The path finder sorts a tile's neighbours by distance and the AI sorts candidate tiles the same way, so it was 11.4% of a 150-turn headless run, the largest single frame in the profile once rule dispatch was fixed.

The nine were never independent: each horizontal candidate depends only on the horizontal wrap and each vertical one only on the vertical, so the shortest of the nine is the shortest horizontal paired with the shortest vertical. Three plus three comparisons, one `hypot`, nothing allocated.

Kept `Math.hypot` over `Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y)`, which measured 20% quicker again: `hypot` is more carefully rounded, the two disagree in the last bit for about a third of all tile pairs, and this feeds sorts that decide where units go. Checked exhaustively against the old implementation over five map sizes and 82,110 tile pairs — bit-identical for every one.
150 turns, measured back to back: 27.9 / 26.7 / 31.3s before, 22.4 / 22.0 / 23.0s after. Conformance checksums unchanged.
Closes #41.

localChanges: release: rule dispatch, and a 150-turn run in a quarter of the time

core-rule@0.1.6 and civ1-unit at ff91905. 150 turns runs in 25.5s against the published artifacts, conformance unchanged, every gate green: 330 packages one copy each, 101 checkouts matching their installed copy, all six suites passing.

log: Movement cost was one rule per cell: one per terrain for moving, and one per (action, terrain) pair for everything else, 132 of those. That reads well and is how rules are meant to compose, but the path finder asks for movement cost once per neighbouring tile it considers, so those 148 rules were the hottest loop in the engine — 21.2 million of the 21.5 million rule validations in a thirty-turn game, 0.7% of which matched. Most were rejected on `action instanceof Action`, before terrain was ever consulted.

The twelve terrains are siblings, so at most one row can match a given terrain and "which rows match" was never a meaningful question. `terrainMovementCost` answers it with a lookup cached by the terrain's constructor, still using `instanceof` so a mod's `class Steppe extends Plains` costs what `Plains` costs.
148 rules per dispatch becomes 16; a 150-turn headless run goes 61.7s → 24.6s. Conformance checksums and RNG draws are unchanged at turns 1, 10 and 50, so the game takes exactly the same decisions.

The per-cell rule ids are gone with the cells: `civ1-unit:unit/movement-cost/move/<Terrain>` is now `…/move`, and `…/action/<Action>/<Terrain>` is now `…/action/<Action>`. Nothing referenced them; a terrain wanting its own cost should have its own row in `baseTerrainMovementCost`, which is still exported.

`RuleRegistry.process` is 98.5% of every rule validation a game performs — 143,148 calls in a thirty-turn headless game, each walking its rule type — and `filter().map()` allocated two closures and two arrays per call for no reason beyond how the line read. `Criteria.validate` did the same with `every`, once per rule per dispatch.

Every rule is still validated before any rule is processed, which is what `filter().map()` did: a rule's effect can change what a later rule's criteria look at, so interleaving the passes would be a behavioural change rather than an optimisation.
Conformance checksums unchanged: 5fa259b4 / f220ec27 / fee4678d.

localChanges: A CPU profile said `Rule.validate` was ~50% of a headless run but could not say whose rules those were: a criterion is an arrow function, so every frame below it is `(anonymous)`. `tools/rule-profile.js` counts dispatch per rule type instead, and answered it outright — `MovementCost` was 21.2M of 21.5M validations in thirty turns, at 148 rules per call, 0.7% matching.

With the matrix collapsed in civ1-unit and the dispatch loops in core-rule freed of their closures, that is 16 rules per call and 2.6M validations, and 150 turns goes 61.7s → 24.6s. The fixture moves only where it should: rule counts 1056 → 924 and `MovementCost` 148 → 16. State checksums and RNG draw counts are identical at turns 1, 10 and 50.
Closes #16.
Stage 7's first wave: core-registry@0.1.3, core-player-world@0.1.13, core-unit-transport@0.1.8 and civ1-unit@0.1.5.
core-registry@0.1.3 (the index mechanism), core-player-world@0.1.13, core-unit-transport@0.1.8 and civ1-unit@0.1.5.

`core-unit-transport` could not be published at all: `Transport.ts` trips TS2742 and TS4094 on its class expression under the scope mapping, and the gate refused — which is how the package came to ship a `TransportRegistry` months older than its source. Its own tsconfig emits correct .js and .d.ts, which is what the commit holds and npm packs, so the gate now carries those two errors for that one file and reports them every run. Any other error still refuses.

Also records the measurement that answers the rest of Stage 7's acceptance: indexing the unit and city registries would buy about 2%, against a core constructor change whose failure mode is a lookup quietly returning the wrong units. Not now.

log: `transportRegistry.getByUnit(unit)` inside a `try`/`catch` was this rule's way of asking "is this unit on a transport?". It answers no by scanning every manifest and throwing a `TypeError`, and the criterion runs for every land unit on every move: 23% of a 150-turn game.
`hasUnit` is a map read that returns `false`. Needs core-unit-transport ^0.1.8.

`get(x, y)` filtered every tile the player had discovered, and `getByTile` did the same — and `register` asks `includes`, which asks `getByTile`, for every visible tile. So a player who had explored more paid more to move, on every move.
Two `Map`s now, by position and by tile. Both are derived from `_tiles`, which is the saved state, so they are transient and rebuilt in `onHydrated`.

Stage 7's mechanism. `index(keyOf)` declares a lookup the registry keeps up to date through `register` and `unregister`; `reindex(entity)` re-files one whose key changed under a live registration, and `remove` falls back to a search for the caller who forgets to.

Built from whatever is already registered, so a subclass can declare one as a field initialiser regardless of order. `get` hands back a copy: a caller that sorts or splices its result must not edit the index.
Measured first, and the measurement was a surprise — see 05-engine-plan.md.

`getByUnit` scans every manifest and answers no by throwing a `TypeError`, and `civ1-unit`'s movement-cost rule asked it that question inside a `try`/`catch` for every land unit on every move: 23% of a 150-turn game.

A manifest's unit and transport are fixed for its lifetime — stowing registers one, unloading unregisters it — so both are safe to index with no `reindex`. `hasUnit` is the question worth asking: a map read that returns `false`.

Only `TransportRegistry`'s own output is committed. `Transport.ts` still trips TS2742, which degrades its `.d.ts` to a stub that would break every consumer, so that file's declaration is left as it was — the error is on `civ typecheck`'s known-failing list and wants fixing on its own.
Needs core-registry ^0.1.3.

localChanges: Stage 7 predicted `getByPlayer`/`getByTile` would dominate. A profile said otherwise: 23% of a 150-turn game was `TransportRegistry.getByUnit`, because `civ1-unit:unit/movement-cost/transported` asks "is this unit aboard anything?" inside a `try`/`catch` — and `getByUnit` answers no by scanning every manifest and throwing a `TypeError`. Every land unit, every move.

`EntityRegistry.index(keyOf)` is the mechanism the stage asks for: a `Map` kept up to date through `register`/`unregister`, with `reindex` for a key that changes under a live registration and a search fallback in `remove` for the caller who forgets. `PlayerWorld` gets the same treatment by hand — it is not a registry — for `get(x, y)` and `getByTile`, both called for every visible tile on every move.
150 turns, 60x40, four players: 91.5s to 71.1s, 22% faster, conformance checksums unchanged throughout.
`tools/bench.js` is how those numbers were taken, profile included, because the stage's acceptance is a number and the first guess about where it came from was wrong.
release: a loaded game applies production again
core-data-object@0.1.17, base-city-yield-gold@0.1.1, core-save-game@0.1.6 and base-goody-hut-gold@0.1.4.
330 packages one copy each, 101 checkouts matching, npm test green with conformance unchanged.

log: Three packages declare a class called `Gold`: this yield, `base-terrain-feature-gold`'s terrain feature and `base-goody-hut-gold`'s action. A save records a class by *name*, so `PlayerTreasury._yield` was written as `{ $class: 'Gold' }` and read back as the terrain feature.

Nothing failed at load. `getByPlayerAndType` found no treasury, threw inside `ProcessYield`, and the whole yield chain died — so a loaded game applied no production, no food and no trade, with nothing to say why. dom111 found it by playing one.

Tagged `GoldYield`; the terrain feature keeps the bare name, because it is a saved entity whose `type` and ids appear in files already written. Registered here because nothing else would: `registerClasses` names the `core-` entity classes and finds the rest through `ConstructorRegistry`s, and a city yield is in neither.
Three packages declare a class called `Gold` and a save records a class by name. See base-city-yield-gold.

`DataObject._keys` is `(keyof this)[]`, so a subclass that adds any public member is not assignable to the base: registering `base-city-yield-gold`'s `Gold` failed with '"values" is not assignable to keyof DataObject', because `Yield` has a `values()`.

The constraint was tighter than the use. This registry reads `name` and `type`, and hands `prototype` to `Object.create` for the hydrator to fill — none of which needs the prototype to be typed as a `DataObject`. Widening, so every existing caller still compiles.

A save records a class by name. Three packages declare a class called `Gold`, so `PlayerTreasury._yield` was written as `{ $class: 'Gold' }` and read back as somebody else's — and the loaded game applied no production, food or trade, because the treasury lookup threw inside `ProcessYield`. The file was byte-perfect; only playing it showed anything wrong.

`encode` now checks, at the point where the name is written and the real class is still in hand, that the name resolves back to that same class. A collision becomes a refusal to save, naming the field, rather than a game that quietly does not work. One offender in a real save: the `Gold` above.
Format 2, because format 1 files carry that ambiguous reference and cannot be resolved after the fact. They are refused with the reason rather than loaded into a game that does not work.

localChanges: The load suite asserted that a loaded game *is* the game that was saved, which was true while it applied no production, food or trade: `PlayerTreasury._yield` came back as the wrong class, the treasury lookup threw inside `ProcessYield`, and the yield chain died. The state round-tripped perfectly. Only playing showed it, and dom111 found it rather than the suite.

So the suite now plays on and requires total build progress across every city to have moved. Before the fix it sat where it was — measured: 4 to 4 across a turn where an uninterrupted run went 4 to 6.

The conformance fixture is re-baselined for the DTO alone: all three state checksums are unchanged, and the DTO moved because ids follow a type tag, so `Gold-1` reads `GoldYield-1`. The byte deltas are exactly that — 195 at turn 10 is 39 ids five characters longer. Translations read the class *name*, which has not changed.
release: gzipped saves and a sensible file name

A turn-1 save was 1.6MB of JSON, and JSON of the most compressible kind: every entity repeats the same field names and most of the file is references like `{"$ref":"Tile-1f4"}`. Gzipped through `CompressionStream` it loses 93% — measured on a real save, 838KB to 55KB — and loading detects the gzip header, so files written either way still open. Without `CompressionStream` the save is written as plain JSON: a save that cannot be written would be worse than a large one.

The name came out as `The English 16x2F09x2F2026.civ-clone.json`. i18next escapes interpolated values for HTML, so the localised date arrived as `16/09/2026`, and stripping the punctuation left `x2F` behind. The default name is built from plain parts now — civilisation, turn and an ISO date — and the sanitiser only removes what a file name cannot hold: `The English, turn 1, 2026-09-16.civ-clone.json.gz`.
Five entries: the save/load UI and the engine fixes it needed — core-turn-based-game@0.1.8, core-world@0.1.16, core-city@0.1.13, core-game@0.1.4 and core-save-game@0.1.5.
core-turn-based-game@0.1.8 (Turn.set), core-world@0.1.16 and core-city@0.1.13 (registry-shaped fields rebuilt on load), core-game@0.1.4 (injectAll) and core-save-game@0.1.5 (restores the turn).
330 packages one copy each, 99 checkouts matching and typechecking, npm test green including the new load suite, conformance unchanged.

log: Same as `World._tiles`: a registry held as a field restores as a plain array, so `city.tiles()` came back unusable.

Only the container is rebuilt. Recomputing the fat cross from the `Tiles` rule would be smaller in the file and would read the *world* — which may not have rebuilt its own tiles yet, because hooks run in no particular order. A hook that puts its own class back around its own restored state cannot depend on another one.

`inject` filled an entity's transient fields, ran its `onHydrated` hook and asserted nothing was left undefined — all three, one entity at a time. That breaks as soon as a hook reads another entity: `City` puts its `Tileset` back and `World` its tile registry, and a city reached before its world threw inside the hook, after a load that had otherwise succeeded.

`injectAll` does the three as sweeps: fill everything, then hooks, then the assertion — which has to come last, since a transient field a hook fills is not missing until every hook has run. `inject` keeps its single-entity behaviour.

Stage 1 took `#private` out of these packages so that `Object.assign` over a created prototype could restore state; the new sweeps went back in with `#` out of habit. They are methods, so nothing about saving changes — but they downlevel to WeakMap helpers, and the publish gate reads those as compiled output that predates its source, which is exactly the check that catches a stale build.
Two things a loaded game needs that only showed up once one was played rather than compared.

The turn is recorded in the file's metadata and the `Turn` is reachable from no entity, so nothing restored it: a game loaded in a fresh process resumed at turn 0 with a turn-40 world. In one process the loaded game adopted the same `Turn` object, so it looked right.
And hydration now injects through `Game.injectAll`, because `City` and `World` rebuild their registry-shaped fields in `onHydrated` and a hook may read any other entity.
The lockfile pinned 0.1.7, which predates `Turn.set`, so the package's own tests failed against the version its range asks for.

A save records the turn in its metadata, and the `Turn` is reachable from no entity, so loading had nothing to restore it from: a game loaded in a fresh process — a reloaded browser tab, which is how the renderer loads one — resumed at turn 0 with a turn-40 world. In one process it looked right only because the loaded game adopted the very `Turn` object the saved one had been counting.
The year needs nothing of its own: `Year.value()` is a function of the turn.

`World._tiles` is an `EntityRegistry` held as a field, and `core-save-game` writes one as an array of its members — the class around a collection is the one thing the format cannot record. So a loaded world arrived with a plain `Tile[]` and `tiles()` handed back an array iterator. Nothing failed at load; the first symptom was `Tileset.from` choking on pairs when something asked a tile for its surroundings, several turns into a game that had loaded fine.
Found by playing a loaded game rather than by comparing its bytes — a save can round-trip byte-identically and still restore a world nobody can play.

localChanges: The engine has been able to save and load for a while and no player could: the menu had no way in. Now "Save Game" writes a file through the browser, and "Load Game" — from the main menu or mid-game — reads one back.
A save leaves as a file rather than into browser storage: it is the player's, it outlives a cleared cache, and it moves between machines.

Loading reloads the page, handing the save over in `sessionStorage`. That is not a storage detail, it is how the engine gets a clean start: plugins register their rules when imported and those rules close over the singleton registries the running game already uses, so a save cannot be laid over a game in progress. A reload gives a new worker with nothing in it, and `src/js/Engine/loadGame.ts` puts the saved game into it — no `engine.start()`, because that is what generates a world.

Resuming picks up from the restored `currentPlayers` rather than firing `turn:start`: the save was taken part way through a turn, and `TurnStart` rules have already run for that player — firing them again would hand back the moves they had spent. A save taken between turns has an empty registry, and then `turn:start` is exactly right.

`buildPluginList.js` now also emits a manifest of package versions, which is what `save` writes into a file and `hydrate` checks it against; without one `save` refuses, since an empty manifest means "cannot check", not "nothing loaded".

`npm run test:load` plays a seeded game, saves it, and loads it in a second process through this same path — two processes, because loading needs an engine that has not started a game. A loaded game is byte-for-byte the game that was saved. Playing on from it still diverges; that is reported rather than asserted, and remains 05-engine-plan.md's last open Stage 5 criterion.

Four of the six had been true for days — round-trip identity, no-op suppression, the compatibility checks — and a fifth is superseded, since pending effects are entities and the refusal it describes is gone.

The two that remain are named as such: replay equivalence, still blocked because plugins register rules at import so a loaded game has none, and the 150-turn size, which has only ever been measured at turn 12.

The first deploy run failed at `npm test`: `Cannot find module '../plugins'`. `src/js/plugins.ts` and `translations.ts` are generated and git-ignored, and `test` ran `ts:compile` before anything generated them. 46 rules now carry an id — `civ1-city:<dir>/<file>/<what it does>`, e.g. `civ1-city:city/created/register` — so a variant can `replace`, `disable`, or order a rule `before`/`after` another by reference instead of outbidding it with a priority number.

Named for what each rule does rather than numbered by position, because a position id breaks the moment a rule is inserted above it. Rules built in a loop take the loop's class names — `${TerrainType.name}` and so on — which survive the production bundle because esbuild runs with `keepNames`.

Raises core-rule to ^0.1.5: 0.1.4 reads a leading string as a priority, so these rules throw `priority(...).value is not a function` against it. The range said `^0.1.0`, which would have let a consumer with an older lockfile install exactly that.

`446c15a` was formatted with prettier 3, which adds trailing commas to parameter lists and call arguments. This package pins prettier 2, whose `prettier:format` removes them again — so the next forced rebuild, in a publish wave or anywhere else, rewrote these files as a side effect.
Formatting only, no behaviour change. Separated from the rule ids that follow so neither diff hides in the other.

`city.player()` was read at assertion time, after `city.capture(enemy)` had reassigned it, so all three assertions compared against the enemy. It passed for years anyway: with `#private` fields two `Player`s had no enumerable state, and deep equality could not tell them apart. Stage 1 made `_id` enumerable and the assertion started meaning something.
The player is captured before the city changes hands. Inverted once to confirm it fails when it should.

`buildCost(Item, cost, 'civ1-unit:city/build-cost')` names each rule `civ1-unit:city/build-cost/Warrior`, so a variant can replace a unit's cost rather than outbid a rule it cannot address. Costs are among the likeliest things a variant changes, and they are all built here, hidden from callers who never see the `new BuildCost(…)`. Without a prefix nothing changes.
Also raises core-rule to ^0.1.5, the first version that accepts an id.

`discharge(effect, ...context)` hands the handler whatever the discharger has in hand that the effect could not carry. A delayed action passes the action it performed, so completion can use the registries that action was constructed with instead of the singletons a handler registered at import reaches for.
A handler must not need it: an effect discharged after a load has only what the save held. Additive — handlers taking one argument are unaffected.

Format 1 was written with a top-level `pendingEffects` array — always empty — and `hydrate` refused a file with anything in it, because effects had no saveable shape until rules had identities. Stage 6 gave them the ordinary one: a `PendingEffect` is a `DataObject` in the `pendingEffects` registry slot, so it travels in `entities` and `registries` like everything else, and both Darwin's Voyage and the ten delayed actions round-trip that way.

So the field is gone from the type and from what `save` writes, and the refusal is gone from `hydrate`. Older files still carry `"pendingEffects": []`, which nothing reads, so the format number stays 1.

The package had a test script and no tests, so the publish gate could only report "not run" — every guarantee it makes was proved in web-renderer's suites instead, against a whole seeded game. These need nothing but a Game and a two-node entity:

encode writes entities as references, classes as names, registry fields as arrays, and round-trips maps and sets through decode; it refuses a nameless function by field path, and decode refuses a dangling reference.
save refuses without a plugin manifest, finds entities no registry lists by following references, and carries a pending effect as an ordinary entity.
hydrate restores a cycle without running a constructor, loads a format-1 file still carrying the old empty placeholder, and a re-save is byte-identical.
assertCompatible refuses an unreadable format and a missing plugin, and reports version drift instead of refusing.

Writing them found one real gap, recorded in the test rather than fixed here: `{ handler: () => {} }.handler` is not anonymous — the property key names it — so a named closure in a field is written as `{ $class: 'handler' }` and fails only on load. Closing that means checking every `$class` against the class registry at save time.
Also corrects the refusal message, which still pointed at Stage 6 for rule identity, and refreshes the lockfile, which predated three of the package's own dependencies.

The completions were closures bound to `this`, so they wrote to the registries the action was constructed with. Converting them to `PendingEffect` handlers moved them to module scope, and six of the ten swapped those registries for `…Instance` singletons. The game never noticed, because `defaultGame` is the singletons; every test with its own registries did. `civ1-unit`'s "should clear Fortified when activated" watched `Fortified` land in a registry it was not looking at.

`delayedBusy` holds the performed action, so it now passes it through `discharge`, and `registerDelayedAction` hands it to `complete` — as a third argument, not the first, so packages written against the two-argument form keep working. After a load there is no performed action, and the `action` factory rebuilds one with defaults, which is all a load can do until plugins register against a game rather than at import.
Requires core-pending-effect with discharge context.

localChanges: `core-rule@0.1.5` gave `Rule` a `private _id` for rule identity, and `DataObject` has its own. TypeScript reduces an intersection of two classes that separately declare a private member of the same name to `never`, so `DataTransferClient`'s data filter — typed to take a `DataObject` — narrowed its `instanceof Busy` branch to `DataObject & Busy` and `npm run build` failed.

The branch is live, not dead: `toPlainObject` hands a filter every field it walks, and `Unit._busy` holds a rule, which this turns into `{ _: 'Fortified' }`. So the parameter is now `DataObject | Busy`, which is what it always received. Type-only; the payload is unchanged.

It got as far as the build because nothing typechecked the renderer's own source: the test suites are bundled with esbuild, which strips types without checking them, and `civ typecheck` compiles the engine checkouts. `npm test` now runs `ts:compile` first, and the release docs say why.

`generate-changelog.mjs` read external changes from the `yarn.lock` diff, and the renderer has resolved through `pnpm-lock.yaml` since b529bae — so every entry since would have listed no engine changes. It now compares the packages resolved at a commit and its parent, from whichever lockfile each has, and looks versions up by `v0.1.x` tag before bare `0.1.x`. A missing tag records the package without a log instead of stopping the run.

Local changes follow the format the release window already renders well: a one-change-per-line message keeps every line, and a subject-and-body message drops the subject and turns each body paragraph into a bullet, with trailers removed. Version-bump commits (`0.1.5`) are left out of external logs.

`--release` (`npm run release:changelog`) adds entries for every commit after the newest one, at the top of `releases.json`, without rewriting any existing entry. `generate-changelog-combined.sh` is retired: it rebuilt the file from scratch, which would delete the hand-written `0.0.0` entry and leave a trailing comma.

Checked against history before trusting it: regenerating 8a11546 reproduced the committed file byte for byte, and 4607766 matched in 32 of 34 packages — the other two are packages marked added, where the old walker kept capturing commits past the release. A trial over the 59 commits since added 59 entries with the existing 52 untouched and no missing tags.

`docs/build-and-release.md` now describes a release end to end: publish and resolve the engine, generate the changelog (it is bundled, so before the build), build on the commit being released, and deploy through civ-clone.github.io to civ.one.

`civ compile` builds a checkout's committed output outside a publish wave, in the publish procedure's format-compile-format order. It matters more than it looks: Node resolves `.js` before `.ts`, so a package's tests run whatever was last compiled, and every civ1 suite went green with named rules in the source and none in what the tests loaded. It refuses a checkout with no local formatter rather than borrowing the renderer's prettier 2, which rewrote 58 files on its first run.

`civ lint` flags a rule registered inside an `Effect` — a closure no save can carry, which is how Darwin's Voyage lost its free advances — whether built inline or bound to a variable first, the spelling Darwin's used. Inverted against the pre-conversion source from git. `civ publish` refuses on a hit.

Tests: the isolation suite checks a delayed action completes into its own game's registry rather than the singleton — the regression six Stage 6 conversions introduced — and the save suite's `pendingEffects` refusal check is now a round trip, since effects travel as entities and the placeholder is gone.
Full reinstall rather than a partial `pnpm update`, which re-resolves only what it names. Picks up core-strategy@0.1.5, core-unit@0.1.22, base-unit-action-goto@0.1.5 and core-save-game@0.1.3.
The packument took 220s to list all four, against a versioned endpoint that answers immediately — pnpm resolves via the packument, so that is the one to wait on.

After: 330 packages one copy each, 99 checkouts matching their installed version, 99 typechecking with no unexpected failure, `civ busy` 14/14, save 17/17, conformance unchanged at 5fa259b4 / f220ec27 / fee4678d.

log: Same gap as `Sleeping`: `BusyRegistry` listed `Stowed` among the states a lookup covers and nothing registered it, so a unit saved aboard a transport failed to load.

`Stowed`'s criterion is `() => false` — it never clears itself; disembarking replaces the busy rule instead. So there is nothing to reconstruct and the factory is the constructor. What keeps the unit on the transport is ordinary saved state on the transport, not this rule.

The last `Busy` state with no way to be rebuilt after a load. It could not be registered before, because the path its criterion compares against was never written to the file — `StrategyNote` was not a `DataObject`, so nothing in `strategyNotes` was saved — and inventing a path on load would have sent the unit somewhere it had not been going.
Two changes make the rule reconstructible:

The note holds the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path`. A note is saved state now, and `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members without recording the class, so a stored `Path` would come back as a plain array with no `end()`. Everything the journey needs is `shift()`, `length` and "the last one", which an array does natively and symmetrically across a save — `moveAlongPath` only ever used the first two. `entries()` returns a copy, so the array is ours to consume.

And the criterion reads the note each time instead of closing over the path, which is what leaves nothing in the rule but the unit. It also covers the note being gone — which happens the moment the unit arrives and `moveAlongPath` unregisters it — so no note means the journey is over and the unit wakes. `Rules/Player/turn-start` already recovered that way at runtime; the rule now agrees with it.

Verified in web-renderer's save suite against a real 12-turn game: a unit put on a journey comes back still following it, the tiles come back as `Tile`s rather than `$ref` strings, ending where they ended before, and the rebuilt rule reports the journey unfinished. The round trip stays byte-identical.

`Pillage` extends `DelayedAction` and was still passing a completion callback to `super.perform`, which now takes a handler identifier. Four consumers stop compiling — `library-unit`, `simple-ai-client`, `simple-world-path` and `civ1-unit` — and at runtime a pillaging unit would register a `PendingEffect` whose handler is a stringified closure, then throw `UnknownHandlerError` when it came due.

It was missed because the grep meant to find every `DelayedAction` subclass searched `node_modules/@civ-clone/*`, which are symlinks into pnpm's store — `grep -r` does not follow symlinks and returned nothing at all. `grep -R` finds eleven, not nine. `Fortify` was missed the same way and found by the same runtime error.

`Pillaging` is new. This action had no `Busy` subclass and used the base `Busy`, which cannot go in `BusyRegistry`: it is keyed by type name, so registering the base would claim the identity for every state that never subclassed it.

`BusyRegistry` named `Sleeping` among the states a lookup covers, but nothing ever registered it. A unit saved asleep therefore failed to load with `UnknownBusyError` — correct behaviour over guessing, but the gap was mine and not the registry's.

Nothing in the rule came from the action: the criterion is "an enemy is visible from where I am" and the effect is "wake up", both read off the unit and the world. Building it inline in `perform`, closing over `this.from()` and the action's own registry, made it look like it held action state. It never did, so `sleeping(unit)` builds it the same way fresh or restored.
`Sleep` extends `DelayedAction` but never calls `super.perform`, so it owes nothing and needs no `PendingEffect` — a plain factory is the whole story.

The grant used to be a one-shot rule registered inside an `Effect`, which registered another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applied to. A closure cannot be written to a file, so a save taken between finishing the wonder and starting the next research lost the two free advances silently — the player never got them and nothing said why.

`building-complete.test.ts` covers the grant. This covers the reason it was rebuilt on `PendingEffect`: that what records the debt now reaches the file, comes back pointing at the restored research, and is still spendable.

Written in web-renderer first, because `core-pending-effect` was unpublished and this package could not install. It belongs here, and it needs no world, no plugin loader and no seeded game to make its point.

The player is deliberately left out of `game.players`: it has no civilisation, and `hydrate`'s claim-replaying pass reads one from every player in that registry. A player without one cannot occur in a real game — `civ1-player` assigns a civilisation as the player is created — so hardening that pass would only hide a genuinely broken save.

"empty at turn 8" was true, and it is also why nobody noticed that `StrategyNote` was not a `DataObject`: the slot was dispositioned as runtime state and saved nothing whatsoever. It is an entity now, and the slot carries `GoTo`'s remaining path as well as AI working memory.

`core-save-game` discovers entities by walking `DataObject`s, and a note was not one — `EntityRegistry<T = any>` has no such constraint, so a registry accepted it happily and nothing ever complained. The result was that `strategyNotes` was dispositioned as runtime state and wrote nothing at all.

Two things were losing data because of it. `GoTo`'s `Busy` criterion compares the unit's tile against the end of the path it is following, and that path is held in one of these — so a unit saved mid-journey could not be restored, and `BusyRegistry` had no way to rebuild the rule. And anything the AI wants to remember across a turn goes here, which means anything it should remember across a save has to be an entity.

`value` stays `Value = any`, but the doc now says what that actually admits: entities, scalars, plain objects, arrays, `Map`s and `Set`s all survive. A class wrapped around a collection does not — `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members and cannot record which class it was — so prefer entities and arrays of them for anything a note must keep.
Three corrections, all found by fixing `Pillage`:
There are fourteen `Busy` identities, not thirteen, and ten are delayed actions rather than eight. `Pillaging` is new.
`Sleeping` and `Stowed` were listed as covered by a lookup and had no factory registered anywhere, so a unit saved asleep or aboard a transport failed to load. Now registered by their own packages.

`GoTo` was described as "looks like the exception and is not", on the grounds that the path it follows is saved as ordinary state. It is not: `StrategyNote` does not extend `DataObject`, so despite `core-save-game` dispositioning `strategyNotes` as `'state'`, no path reaches the file and the criterion cannot be rebuilt. A unit saved mid-journey fails to load. That is the honest answer until either `StrategyNote` becomes saveable or `GoTo` keeps its path somewhere that is.

Also records why counting these by hand beats grepping for them: `grep -r` does not follow symlinks, and `node_modules/@civ-clone/*` are symlinks into pnpm's store, so `-r` for `extends DelayedAction` finds nothing whatsoever.

It took two changes elsewhere: `StrategyNote` became a `DataObject`, so the path it holds is written to the file at all, and `base-unit-action-goto` now stores the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path` — `encode` writes a registry held as a field as an array of its members and cannot record the class around it.

localChanges: `GoTo` was the last `Busy` state that could not be rebuilt after a load, and the fix reached across three packages — `StrategyNote` became a `DataObject`, `base-unit-action-goto` stores the remaining `Tile`s rather than the `Path`, and the busy factory is registered. This is the check that the three of them add up to a restored journey.

Built here rather than by issuing a real `GoTo`, so it does not depend on the AI happening to order one, but with the pieces `GoTo.perform` uses including its exported factory.
