`01-constraints.md` §4's one unserialisable continuation. It granted two free research completions by registering a one-shot rule that registered another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applied to — so the only record of the grant was a closure in the rule registry, and a save taken between finishing the wonder and starting the next research lost it silently. The player simply never got their advances.

What records it now is a `PendingEffect` against the player's research: "owed two completions". The rule that spends them, `Rules/PlayerResearch/started`, is registered at import like every other rule — which is also why this stops needing `ruleRegistry.register` inside an `Effect`, the pattern Stage 6 adds a lint rule against.

Partly-paid debts write the remainder back rather than discharging, because discharging forgets — and a save taken between the first completion and the second would then lose the second. The last one discharges, which removes the debt and applies it.

The test for the grant now registers the rule it depends on, which it could not before: the rule did not exist until the wonder's effect created it. That is the same lesson `civ1-city`'s suite taught — a test should declare every input it relies on.

Verified end to end in the renderer: 9/9 in `npm run test:darwins`, and the conformance checksums are unchanged. The rule-count instrument moved from 1,055 to 1,056 with `Started` going 1 → 2, which is exactly right: one permanent rule at import in place of one-shots at runtime.

A `pendingEffects` slot, per-game like everything else. It holds what the game owes its entities — a unit part-way through building a road, a player owed free research — as saveable records rather than closures.

`Game` holds a `pendingEffects` slot, so its own tests could not run until that package was published — which is why the publish gate stopped here rather than half-publishing the wave. This package tracks its lockfile, so the resolution is part of the commit.
The engine has two unserialisable continuations and they looked like separate problems:

**A delayed action.** `DelayedAction.perform` closes over `endTurn = turn.value() + turns` and a completion callback, so a unit three turns into building a road holds its remaining work entirely in a closure.
**Darwin's Voyage.** It grants two free research completions by registering a one-shot rule that registers another one-shot rule, each closing over the `PlayerResearch` it applies to.

Both are the same thing: a **debt owed to a target entity**. "This unit is owed the completion of a road at turn 41." "This player's research is owed two free completions." The closures implement the debt; only the debt needs saving. `01-constraints.md` §4 took Darwin's Voyage to be the engine's one unserialisable continuation — it is one of nine, since eight unit actions go through `DelayedAction`.

**There is deliberately no trigger.** Modelling *when* an effect is due — a turn, an event, a condition — is the obvious next move and the wrong one: it would be a second, weaker scheduler beside the one the engine already has. A package registers an ordinary rule, once at import, that watches whatever it cares about and discharges the effects that have come due. Leaving timing out is exactly what lets one class cover both cases:
build road       …build-road:complete   Unit            endTurn     the Busy criterion Darwin's Voyage  civ1-wonder:darwins…   PlayerResearch  remaining   a Started rule

`handler` is a string so the closure stays in the plugin and the file holds only a name. `target` is a `DataObject` so it saves as a `$ref` and comes back as the restored instance — typed as the base class, because a debt is owed to a `Unit`, a `PlayerResearch` or anything else and nothing here needs to know which.

`discharge` unregisters *before* applying, and the test says why twice over: a handler that owes a follow-up must not have it removed by the discharge that caused it, and an effect whose handler throws must not be retried every turn for ever.

`DataObject` declares `_keys: (keyof this)[]`, and that polymorphic `this` makes no subclass assignable to the base — passing a `Unit` fails on `'player' is not assignable to keyof DataObject`. The public interface says everything this needs and has no such problem.
Stage 6 of the engine serialisation plan, and the answer to 02-design-review.md §3: "208 `Rule` subclasses exist across the tree. Not one rule instance has a name, an id, or a declared origin."
`Rule`'s constructor now accepts a leading string. It is optional, so this lands package by package and the 1,055 rules a real game registers keep working untouched.

**Strings rather than subclasses, and the numbers decide it.** A real game registers 1,055 rule *instances* across 163 classes. Naming an instance is the thing `replace`, `disable`, `before` and `after` need, and no amount of subclassing provides it — you cannot subclass 1,055 times, and the second instance of any class is unaddressable either way. Subclasses answer "what kind of rule is this", which the engine already has and already uses well.
`RuleRegistry` gains `getById`, `replace`, `disableById`, `enableById`, `before` and `after`.

**`before`/`after` reposition rather than compute a priority.** Giving a rule `target.priority() - 1` looks simpler and is wrong twice: `Normal` is 2000 for almost everything, so "one less" collides with whatever else sits there, and it breaks silently when the target's priority later changes. Position is what `before` means, so position is what gets set — after the existing priority sort, which `Array.prototype.sort` keeps stable. Rules with no constraint take an early return, so the hot path is exactly as cheap as before.

**Every id-taking method throws on an unknown id.** A plugin that means to replace `civ1-city:city/grow` and mistypes it should fail at load, not run a game where its override silently never applied — which is the failure mode strings invite and the reason to guard it. Two rules claiming one id is refused at registration for the same reason `ClassRegistry` refuses two classes: the loser would be unaddressable.

The test for two rules constrained against one target caught a real bug: inserting each at `index + 1` made the second land before the first, so they came out reversed. They are grouped and spliced as a unit now, with priority deciding within a group.

The publish gate reported it: "a forced rebuild reformats 3 file(s); the commit is what gets published". The emitted `.js` and its map described the pre-prettier source, because this package was built before the format-compile-format ordering was applied to it — the same drift that 23 of Stage 4's commits carried, and that `lib/procedure.js` and `tools/stage4.js` were both changed to prevent.

Behaviour is identical either way; the artifact simply did not match the `.ts` beside it, which is exactly the kind of thing that survives every gate. A second format-compile-format pass now changes nothing.

**A real game now saves and loads byte-identically.** Turn 12 of the conformance game: 6,499 entities, 23 registries, 57KB gzipped; saved, loaded into a fresh game, saved again, and the two files are identical. That is the check that catches a dropped field, and it passes.
Three pieces made it work.

`pendingEffects` is a saved registry. The debts are entities; the handlers that discharge them are functions registered at import and are never saved, which is the whole point — a closure cannot be written to a file.

`Unit._busy` encodes as `{ $busy: '<class>' }`. It is the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — measured: 1,055 registered rules, 4,007 reachable entities, two fields. A rule is a closure, but *which* rule is a name, and every `Busy` subclass carries no instance state: anything that varies, like when a delayed action finishes, now lives in a `PendingEffect`.

`hydrate` resolves those markers in a pass of its own, after the fill. Rebuilding one needs the entity that holds it, and `decode` walks a field's value with no idea whose field it is. The order matters: the pending effects are filled by the pass before, so a factory asking when a road finishes can read it.
`$busy` is a distinct marker rather than a `$class` because a class reference decodes to the class, and what a unit needs back is an *instance*, built for it by the package that owns it.
`test:save` is wired into `npm test` now that it passes, and the registry-membership assertion compares a summary rather than printing several thousand ids on every run.

`Unit._busy` is the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — measured: 1,055 registered rules, 4,007 reachable entities, exactly two fields, both `<Unit>._busy`. A rule is a closure, so `core-save-game` refuses to encode one, and that single field is what blocks saving.

`BusyRegistry` maps a `Busy` identity to a factory that rebuilds it for a unit. A factory rather than the class, because construction is where the meaning is: `Fortified` is built with `new Criterion(() => false)` at the call site, `Stowed` builds its own, and `GoTo`'s criterion closes over the unit and its path.

This covers five of the thirteen `Busy` subclasses — `Fortified`, `Fortifying`, `Stowed`, `Sleeping`, `GoTo` — whose criteria are pure functions of the world and the unit, and whose durable facts are saved separately. `Fortify` registers a `Fortified` *`UnitImprovement`* alongside the busy rule, and that is ordinary state.

**It cannot cover the other eight, and the class comment says so rather than leaving someone to find out.** They come from `DelayedAction.perform`, which closes over `endTurn = turn.value() + turns` and the completion `action`. `endTurn` says when the work finishes; `action` says what it does. Neither is derivable from the unit, so a factory would have to invent a completion turn — and a unit three turns into building a road would load either finished or never finishing.

That is the same problem `PendingEffect` exists for: a delayed action *is* "at turn N, do X", which is exactly the handler-plus-data shape 03-save-format.md defines. Darwin's Voyage was taken to be the only unserialisable continuation in the engine. It is one of nine.

`DelayedAction.perform` took a completion callback and now takes a handler identifier. That callback was a closure, and `Unit._busy` — the only field in the engine that holds a `Rule` — held a rule built around it. `core-save-game` refused to encode it, so a unit three turns into building a road could not be saved at all.

`perform` now registers a `PendingEffect` carrying the turn the work comes due, and `delayedBusy` builds the `Busy` rule from *that*. One function, called from two places — `perform` when the action starts and `BusyRegistry` when a save is loaded — because if the two built the rule separately they would drift, and the drift would only appear in a loaded game.

`registerDelayedAction` pairs the two registrations a package needs: the handler that says what finishing does, and the factory that rebuilds the in-progress rule. Split across two call sites they would be easy to half-do, and a package with a handler but no factory produces a unit that loads idle while still owing the work. The action is rebuilt by a factory rather than `new ActionType(...)` because the constructors genuinely differ — `ClearForest` takes a `TerrainFeatureRegistry` where `BuildIrrigation` takes a `Turn`.

**One latent bug fixed on the way.** The criterion compared `turn.value() === endTurn`, so a unit whose completion turn slipped past — a skipped turn, or a save loaded on a later turn — stayed busy for ever with nothing to say why. It is `>=` now, which cannot get stuck and agrees on the turn it is due.
Conformance is unchanged across the nine delayed actions, and a turn-12 save round-trips byte-identically.

Two findings from publishing the Stage 6 wave.

`registry.npmjs.org/<pkg>/<version>` returned 200 for `core-pending-effect@0.1.1` while the packument still listed no versions at all, and pnpm resolves via the packument — so `pnpm install` failed with "not in the npm registry" against a version that demonstrably existed, and left a lockfile that had to be cleared before the retry worked. Verify a publish against the versioned endpoint; wait on the packument before installing.

Separately, `civ1-wonder` has nine test files and no installed `ts-mocha`, so its suite had never run. The gate's distinction between "the test script cannot run" and "the tests failed" is what surfaced it — and comparing an unrun suite against its parent commit has to be done the same way both times, since these suites share singleton registries and give a different failure run alone than run together.

It lived here only because `core-pending-effect` was unpublished and `civ1-wonder` could not install. Now four `chai` assertions in `civ1-wonder/tests/darwins-voyage-save.test.ts` say what the 9-check harness said, in 12ms and without a seeded game — a suite only needs the renderer when it needs a whole loaded game, and this one never did.

Also records `civ1-wonder`'s one failing test as known and pre-existing: `City.yield` wants 6 trade from Colossus and gets 4. Verified by running the suite at `9e92866^` — 38 passing, 1 failing, the same assertion, the same numbers — and the test imports neither module that commit touched. It only surfaced now because the package had no `ts-mocha`, so its suite had never run at all.

Registers classes at `engine:start`, before players are created, for the reason the save suite already documents: `civ1-player` unregisters a civilisation once a player claims it, so a registry read afterwards is missing every civilisation in the game. Getting that wrong is what `Unknown entity type 'Aztec'` looks like.

The fixture's rule count moves from 1,055 to 1,056 with `Started` going 1 → 2. The checksums do not move. That is the instrument reporting exactly what changed: one permanent rule registered at import, in place of one-shot rules registered at runtime — which is the whole point of the change.

**Strings over subclasses, decided by the numbers.** 1,055 rule instances across 163 classes. `replace`/`disable`/`before`/`after` need to name one *instance*, and subclassing cannot — you would need 1,055 subclasses, and the second instance of any class stays unaddressable. **`01-constraints.md` §4 said Darwin's Voyage was the one unserialisable continuation in the engine. It is one of nine.**

`Unit._busy` is the only field anywhere that holds a `Rule` — 1,055 rules, 4,007 entities, two fields. Five of the thirteen `Busy` subclasses need only an identity and a factory: their criteria are pure functions of the world and the unit, and the durable facts are saved separately.

The other eight come from `DelayedAction.perform`, which closes over `endTurn` and the completion `action`. `Rule` now carries an `_id`, and a rule is reachable from an entity through `Unit._busy` — so `_id: null` appears in the DTO and the state digest for every fortified unit. 99 bytes at turn 10, 792 at turn 50, and turn 1 is untouched because nothing is fortified yet.

The three things `core-save-game` needs from here, per Stage 5 of the engine serialisation plan.

**`typeNameOf(Class)`** returns an explicit `static type` when a class declares one and `constructor.name` otherwise, and `idProvider` now keys on it. Identical behaviour today — nothing declares a tag — which is what makes it safe to land alone, and it means ids follow the tags whenever 02-design-review.md §7 rolls them out. That rollout is 303 classes across 243 packages, so it is deliberately not a prerequisite for saving.

It reads an *own* `type`, not an inherited one. `static` members are inherited, so `Class.type` on a subclass of a tagged class returns the parent's tag — every descendant of one tagged class would save, load and take ids as that parent, an entity type swallowing a hierarchy. Caught by the test for it, and the same trap `allTransient()` walks the prototype chain to avoid.

**`idCounters()` / `restoreIdCounters()`** expose the per-class counters a save has to carry. Without them the first entity created after a load takes an id a loaded entity already holds — `City-1` twice, one of them unreachable — and nothing throws. Restoring only ever moves a counter *forward*, because plugin imports create terrain definitions, civilisations and leaders before a save is loaded, and lowering a counter would hand out ids those already hold.

**`ClassRegistry`** maps type name to class for hydration, which allocates with `Object.create(Type.prototype)` and never calls a constructor. It refuses two classes claiming one name, and refuses a name of one character — which is what `keepNames: false` would produce, and saves written then would be unreadable by any other build. §7's explicit tags are the real fix; this makes the failure a startup error instead of a corrupt file. It cannot false-positive: the shortest real class name in the engine is `Or`, at two characters, and that is a rule combinator.

`typeNameOf` is a free function rather than `static typeName()` because the static version was written first and `ConstructorStaysAssignable` rejected it immediately — a required static, method or property, stops `IConstructor<T>` satisfying `typeof T`. That is what 0.1.14 shipped, and the guard caught the second attempt within a minute.

`save.engine.plugins` needs every loaded package and its exact version, for the three-tier compatibility check in 03-save-format.md: refuse a missing plugin, allow an extra one, warn on a version change.

Nothing announced itself before this. Plugins load as bare side-effect imports from a list the host generates, so there was no manifest to read back at all. The alternative was 123 packages each registering their own name and version; instead the host that generated the import list registers the whole manifest, because it is the one place that already knows both and cannot drift out of step with the imports it wrote.

An empty manifest therefore means "cannot check", not "nothing loaded" — a distinction `core-save-game` acts on by refusing to write a save without one, rather than emitting a file that silently cannot be validated.
No tests here: this package has no runner, and adding mocha, chai and ts-mocha for two accessors is not worth it. `core-save-game`'s compatibility tests exercise them end to end.

Stage 5 of the engine serialisation plan. `stateKeys()` omits every transient field, so an entity rebuilt with `Object.assign(Object.create(Type.prototype), state)` arrives with those fields *absent* — not null, not empty, `undefined`. Measured against a real game, three of the four categories then misbehave and one does so silently:
Yield.value()          undefined   (real value 3, and no error) Tile.getNeighbours()   throws City.toPlainObject()   throws

`Yield` is the dangerous one. Its guard is `if (this._valueCache === null)`, which is false for `undefined`, so the recompute never runs and every yield in a loaded game reads empty. Nothing reports it.
So `inject` has three tables rather than the one the design assumed:

**collaborators** — registries, `turn`, `year`, and the game's `rng` for a `() => number` field. Sixteen entries, two of them spellings of the same thing (`_ruleRegistry` and `_rulesRegistry` both exist).
**caches** — the value the field's own initialiser would have produced: `[]`, `null`, `new Map()`. Five entries.

**derived** — from the game *and* the entity's restored state, so neither table can express them. `Civilization._attributes` is a filtered view of the game's; `World._generator` is rebuilt from the world's own saved height and width, which is exact because every geometry method is a pure function of those two and a loaded world never calls `generate()`.

**The assertion at the end matters more than the tables.** A transient field added later and not added here leaves `undefined` behind, so `inject` throws naming the class and the field. That is what turns the next `Yield` into a load failure instead of a wrong answer.

`_id` and `_keys` are skipped deliberately: they are transient but come from the save, beside the entity id rather than inside `state`. `_keys` cannot come from here at all — constructors build it with `addKey()`, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws and a loaded game sends nothing to the renderer.
An optional `onHydrated()` hook runs last. Exactly one class in the 328 packages needs it.

Also: a `classes: ClassRegistry` slot, per-game like everything else. It lives in `core-data-object` rather than `core-save-game` as the plan had it — that placement is a dependency cycle, since `core-save-game` depends on `core-game`.
`core-data-object` moves to ^0.1.16, the version `ClassRegistry` and `allTransient()` exist in.
Two slots, `availableTileImprovements` and `availableUnitImprovements`, alongside the existing `availableTerrainFeatures` and `availableCityBuildItems`.

They exist because nothing held the tile and unit improvement *classes* — `tileImprovements` and `unitImprovements` hold what has been built and acquired. A save records `Irrigation`, `Road` and `Fortified` by name and had nothing to resolve them against.
`core-tile-improvement` 0.1.3 → 0.1.4 and `core-unit-improvement` 0.1.2 → 0.1.3, the versions that contain `AvailableTileImprovementRegistry` and `AvailableUnitImprovementRegistry`.

`Game` imports both, so its own tests could not run until they were published — which is why the publish gate stopped here on the first pass rather than half-publishing the wave. This package tracks its lockfile, unlike most, so the resolution is part of the commit.

`PlayerTile` is the only class in all 328 packages that builds per-instance structure in its constructor: it installs an accessor per registered `AdditionalData` with `Object.defineProperty`, and calls `addKey()` with a non-literal argument. Every other class's state is either saved or supplied by the `Game`.

Those accessors are non-enumerable, so `stateKeys()` never sees them and a save never carries them. A hydrated `PlayerTile` would therefore have `_keys` naming methods that do not exist, and `toPlainObject()` walks `keys()` calling each one — so the first thing to break would be the payload sent to the renderer.

`onHydrated()` is the hook `Game.inject` calls last if a class defines one. One class needs it, so it is a hook rather than a convention. `setAdditionalData` takes a flag because the keys come back with the save and re-adding them would duplicate every one.

Stage 5 of the engine serialisation plan, implementing 03-save-format.md. `save` walks the registries holding runtime state and records every entity's non-transient fields; `hydrate` allocates each with `Object.create(Type.prototype)` — never a constructor, so nothing re-emits `city:created` — fills it, then hands it to `Game.inject` for the collaborators and caches a file cannot carry.
Measured on a real four-player 60x40 game at turn 12: **6,499 entities, 837KB of JSON, 57KB gzipped**, against a budget of 1MB gzipped at turn 150. Loading emits no creation events.
Four things here differ from the document, each for a reason:

**`ClassRegistry` lives in `core-data-object`.** The layout in the plan puts it here while `hydrate` reads it as `game.classes`, which would make `core-game` depend on this package — and this package depends on `core-game`.

**`SerialisedEntity` carries `keys` beside `id`.** `_keys` is built by `addKey()` calls inside constructors, so no `Game` can supply it, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws and a loaded game sends the renderer nothing. Putting it in `state` instead would mean removing `_keys` from `DataObject.transient`, moving the conformance checksum for something that is bookkeeping rather than state.

**Registry dispositions are exhaustive at compile time.** `registries.ts` types its table as `Record<keyof GameSlots, Disposition>`, so adding a slot to `Game` fails to compile here until someone says whether it is saved. The classifications come from measuring a real game rather than reading names: `terrainFeatures` reads like a mixed registry and is not — its definitions are classes in `availableTerrainFeatures` and every entry is a placed instance. `save` additionally refuses a `state` registry that turns out to hold a class, and `hydrate` refuses membership for a slot that is not state, because loading it would register duplicates over the definitions plugin imports already created.

**Entities are discovered breadth-first, not taken from registries.** `World` is reachable only through `Tile._map` and a `Tile` only through `World._tiles`; neither is in a `Game` registry, so a pass over the registries alone writes a save full of `$ref`s to nothing.
`pendingEffects` refuses rather than drops: restoring one needs rule identity, and silently discarding a queued continuation loses it with no symptom.
Two changes, both driven by what the acceptance test measured rather than by reading the tree.

`Yield` subclasses are constructed directly and appear in no registry, so each `core-` one has to be named explicitly. `Moves` and `FoodStorage` turned up as unresolvable entity types in a twelve-turn save; the rest are here because the next longer game would have found them one at a time.

`core-science/Yields/Research` is deliberately *not* among them, and the reason is worth recording: three classes are named `Research` — that one, `base-city-yield-research`'s byte-identical `class Research extends Yield {}`, and `base-trade-rate-research`'s `TradeRate`. Registering a fourth claimant displaces whichever got there first, which today is the trade rate. So a save naming `Research` already resolves to the wrong kind of thing, and adding to the pile makes it worse. Tags would fix it; which of the two identical `Yield`s is the real one is a modelling question, not a naming one.

`registerClasses` also takes a `collisions` array now. Throwing on the first ambiguous name made the rest invisible — there were five, and only the first was ever visible. A collected name is simply absent from the registry, so a save using it fails to load rather than loading the wrong class, and a host can report the whole list.

Harvesting classes from definition registries is restricted to `attributes` and `traits` rather than derived from the disposition. Doing it for every definition registry reaches `rules`: 1,055 `Rule` instances whose names collide 271 times over and not one of which is ever a saved entity.
With those in place, a twelve-turn save resolves 72 of its 75 entity types. The three that remain — `Fortified`, `Irrigation`, `Road` — are `base-` packages listed in no registry at all.

Two new dispositions for `availableTileImprovements` and `availableUnitImprovements`, which is all it took for **every one of the 75 entity types in a real save to resolve** — the three that did not (`Irrigation`, `Road`, `Fortified`) were in no registry, and now are. Zero ambiguous names remain, after `RailroadAdvance` was tagged: adding the tile improvement registry made `Railroad` collide with the advance, which nothing had noticed because the class had never been registered anywhere.

`encode` now refuses a function with no name rather than writing `{ $class: '' }`. Such a thing could never be decoded, and the failure would land on whoever loaded the file rather than whoever wrote it. The message carries the field path, which is how the one case that reaches it got identified:
Cannot encode Warrior._busy._criteria._criteria.[0]._criterion

That is `Unit._busy` holding a `Busy` rule, and a rule is a closure. `05-engine-plan.md` predicted exactly this and named the fix: `busy` has to serialise as a rule *identity*, which needs Stage 6's named rules. Refusing is the deliberate choice — the alternative is a save that loads with every fortified unit silently un-fortified.
So saving is now blocked on one field, which is a better place to be than blocked on a category.

`Research` had three claimants and resolved to whichever reached a registry first — the trade rate. With `base-city-yield-research` now re-exporting `core-science`'s class and the trade rate tagged `ResearchTradeRate`, the name is unambiguous and can be registered.
257 classes, zero ambiguous names, all 75 entity types in a real save resolve.

`TileImprovementRegistry` holds the improvements that have been *built* — instances, per tile. Nothing held the classes a ruleset offers, which left them reachable only through the `Available` rule: enough to decide what a unit may build, and not enough for anything that needs to enumerate them.

Saving is what exposed it. A save records `Irrigation` and `Road` by name, and hydration had no way to turn either back into a class — they were two of the three entity types in a real save that resolved to nothing at all.
Mirrors `AvailableTerrainFeatureRegistry` exactly, including the ruleset-registers-them convention: `civ1-world/registerTileImprovements` fills it, not the five `base-tile-improvement-*` packages.

`UnitImprovementRegistry` holds the improvements a unit has *acquired*: instances, per unit. The classes — `Fortified`, `Veteran` — were reachable only through the rules that grant them, so nothing could enumerate them and a save recording `Fortified` by name could not resolve it.
Mirrors `AvailableTileImprovementRegistry`, added alongside it for the same reason.

This rebuilds live entities from a real game exactly as the hydrator's passes 1 and 2 do — `stateKeys()` for the state, `_id` and `_keys` carried beside it — then injects and calls the accessor that broke:

Yield.value()                   3          (was undefined, silently) Tile.getNeighbours()            works      (threw) City.toPlainObject()            works      (threw) City.keys()                     works      (undefined) World.get()                     works      (no generator was saved) Civilization.attributes()       works      (a derived registry) PlayerTile.toPlainObject()      works      (accessors reinstalled)
15 checks, wired into `npm test`. Two of them are worth calling out:

`Year.value()` asserts *parity with the original* rather than a value. A bare `Game` has no `YearRule`, so the original throws too — asserting a number would have been asserting the fixture rather than the behaviour, and the contract here is that a hydrated entity behaves as the one it was rebuilt from.

The last check inverts the guard: a class whose `transient` names a field `inject` has no source for must make the load fail, naming the field. It asserts on the message, so a throw for the wrong reason does not pass.

Writing this found two defects in itself rather than in `inject` — a `Year(turn, ruleRegistry)` constructor called with the arguments the wrong way round, and a `City` whose player had no civilisation, which `toPlainObject()` reaches for and throws on. Both worth noting because both looked like hydration failures at first.
Three findings, each measured against a real game rather than reasoned about, by rebuilding live entities from `stateKeys()` alone — exactly what the documented hydrator's passes 1 and 2 produce.

The design assumed every transient field is "a registry the `Game` holds". The Stage 4 declarations disagree: they also contain caches, `DataObject` bookkeeping, and one class's derived accessors. `transient` means "not saved", which is a wider category than "supplied by the `Game`".

Caches need their *initialiser*, not a collaborator, and the guards are written against it — `if (this._valueCache === null)` is false when the field is absent, so `Yield.value()` returns `undefined` with no error and every yield in a loaded game reads empty. `Tile.getNeighbours()` and `Year` fail the same way but throw. So `inject` needs a table of five empties, and more importantly an assertion that no transient field is left `undefined` — which is what turns a future cache field into a load failure rather than a wrong answer.

`_keys` cannot be injected at all: it is built by `addKey()` calls inside constructors, and without it `toPlainObject()` throws, so a loaded game sends nothing to the renderer. It belongs beside `id` in `SerialisedEntity`, not in `state` — putting it in `state` would mean removing it from `DataObject.transient`, which moves the conformance checksum for something that is bookkeeping rather than state.
`PlayerTile` is the only class in 328 packages that builds per-instance structure in its constructor. One class, so one optional `onHydrated()` hook rather than a convention.

Also recorded for Stage 5: why `ClassRegistry` went into `core-data-object` rather than `core-save-game` (the documented placement is a dependency cycle), and why §7's `static type` is not a prerequisite — 303 classes across 243 packages, 210 uncloned, against a failure mode `ClassRegistry` can refuse outright for one method's worth of code.

Nothing failed in this package either way: its own tests pass, and they still do. That is the whole reason this shipped, so the guard is a compile-time assertion rather than a test — `Assert<IConstructor< DataObject> extends typeof DataObject ? true : false>` fails with TS2344 the moment a required static is added again. Verified by putting the required declaration back and watching it fire.
`allTransient()` already read the member as `transient?: readonly string[]` behind an `Array.isArray` check, so the optional type costs nothing at runtime and the mechanism is unchanged.

localChanges: `core-data-object@0.1.14` added one required static to `DataObject` and stopped 22 of the 83 checkouts typechecking. Nothing in `core-data-object` failed: its own tests passed either side, the publish gate ran them, the renderer's suites stayed green because esbuild does not typecheck, and the conformance checksums did not move. The defect lived entirely in two call sites in other packages.

Every other gate here is per-package, so none of them could see it. `civ typecheck` compiles each checkout against the renderer's installed tree — the one place all 328 packages resolve — in about a minute.

It rebuilds with `--force` and then restores each checkout, so it refuses to run against a tree with modified tracked files rather than reverting work it did not cause. Three pre-existing failures are listed by name with the reason and the version they were verified against, and a package that starts passing is reported so a stale entry cannot hide the next real one — the rule `KNOWN_FAILING_TESTS` earned.

The last Stage 4 item, in a commit that does nothing else — which is the point. `7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b` held unchanged through Stages 1, 2 and 3, and that is exactly what let each of them claim it changed nothing. Widening ends that comparability, so the discontinuity gets one cause and this message is it.

New baseline: `aebaf5c2 / af0ade7e / f6e495ff`, from 2,459 entities and 9,729 fields at turn 1 rising to 2,490 and 9,970 by turn 50, via `DataObject.stateKeys()`. Deterministic across runs and across processes.

`snapshots.*.state` records the entity and field counts beside the hash, so a drift says how much moved rather than only that something did. Demonstrated by removing `_ruleRegistry` from `City`'s declaration — the failure Stage 4 exists to prevent: turn 10 goes from 9,793 fields to 9,796 and turn 50 from 9,970 to 9,976, one per city, with turn 1 untouched because no city exists yet. Every other part of the snapshot is identical under that change, which is why the narrow subset could not have caught it.

References are by id, because `City._tile` reaches the `World` and through it every tile. Anything that is neither a primitive nor a `DataObject` reduces to its class name — honest rather than complete, and those fields (`Unit._busy`, `Unit._status`, `PlayerTreasury._yield`) are the ones waiting on Stage 6's named rules.
The instruments stay outside the hash as before: the DTO digest, `mathRandomCalls` and the rule counts. `state` is inside it, because it is not an instrument — it is the measurement.

Same defect as `lib/procedure.js` had, reintroduced by writing a new driver: it compiled and then formatted, so the emitted `.js` and its map described the pre-prettier source. ts-morph writes `static readonly transient = ['_a', '_b', '_c'];` on one line and prettier wraps it past 80 columns, so 23 of the 24 rollout commits held a `.js` with the one-line array against a `.ts` with the wrapped one.

Harmless in itself — the same array either way — and that is the point: it compiles, it tests, it publishes, and the artifact simply does not match its source. The 23 commits have been rebuilt and amended, and a second format/compile/format pass over all 24 now changes nothing.

`tools/stage4.js` applies the transient codemod across the 24 packages, raises each one's core-data-object range to the version the declaration is read in, compiles, formats, syncs and commits. `--all` asks the codemod which packages have something to declare rather than reading the manifest, which records work *remaining* and so shrinks as the rollout proceeds.
Two codemod corrections, both found by reviewing the derivation against the source rather than against itself:

`CACHE_NAMES` was `_(.*Cache|cached.*|neighbours)`, which needs a character before a capital `Cache` — so it matched `_yieldCache` and `_valueCache` but not a bare `_cache`. `core-game-year`'s `Year._cache` is a turn-to-year memo and was classified as state.

`World._generator` is a `Generator`, which the `Game` supplies through `generators` but which only `implements IGenerator` — so it can be neither saved as an entity reference nor rebuilt from one. The obvious generalisation is wrong: `City` is also a member of a `Game` registry and `CityGrowth._city` must certainly be saved. The difference is that `City` is a `DataObject`, so this is a judgement per type and there is an explicit list of one. `Rule` descendants are deliberately not on it: `Unit._busy` is equally unsaveable but is real state, and wants Stage 6's rule identities rather than being dropped.

`tests/engine/transient.ts` is the acceptance check. A declaration is a list of strings, so nothing about it proves the field exists or that `stateKeys()` acts on it — a typo reads correctly and does nothing. It asserts on real instances that the names are real fields, that `allTransient()` stays additive across the prototype chain, that state survives, and that `stateKeys()` is narrower than `Object.keys()` at all. Verified by spelling `_neighbours` the American way and watching two checks fail.

The wave published cleanly (civ1-city 0.1.2, civ1-city-improvement 0.1.3, core-data-object 0.1.14, all verified against the registry and the pushed tags). Reinstalling the renderer against it exposed two tree problems, both of which had been quietly true for several stages.

`civ duplicates` finds any @civ-clone package with more than one live copy, by store entry rather than by version — the duplicated copies are often the *same* version, which is what made this invisible. Two copies are two modules, so a class from one is never `instanceof` the same class from the other, and nothing reports it. `civ publish` now runs it first and refuses on a hit, since `resolutionOf` reads that tree to decide npm-versus-git-push.

`civ stale` compares each installed copy against its checkout. This one found a false claim of mine: the committed lockfile pinned `core-turn-based-game@0.1.6` and `civ1-player@0.1.1` — the commits immediately before each `registerEvents` change — so every suite run cited as Stage 3 evidence used pre-change copies of exactly the two packages that stage's second half touched. With them installed the checksums are still 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b and isolation is 13/13, so the change is behaviour-preserving; it is now measured rather than assumed. It defaults to every checkout, not the manifest, which records work *remaining* and lists 18 of 84.

The cause of both was this document's own post-wave step, `pnpm update '@civ-clone/*'`. A partial update re-resolves only what it names, and each publish of a GitHub-resolved package changes its tarball hash, so the renderer had accumulated three `civ1-city` tarballs, one per stage that published it. Replaced with a full re-resolve.

Also recorded: `npm publish` can return 202 Accepted with "being processed", so the registry 404s the new version for a minute. That is a third state beyond the two the gate knows, and `release()` pipes npm's stdio — read ~/.npm/_logs, not the wave log.

Three separate defects, all of them the tests leaning on global state:

`created.test.ts` and `grow.test.ts` built every registry except `WorkedTileRegistry`, so `assignWorkers` wrote into the singleton and tripped over tiles another file had already claimed. Threading a local registry through `cityCreated`/`cityGrow` is not enough on its own: the no-argument `WorkedTileRegistry` constructor captures the *singleton* `RuleRegistry`, so `tileCanBeWorkedBy` found no `CanBeWorked` rule, and `[].every(...)` is `true` — every tile read as workable, including the ones already worked. `build.test.ts` was flaky before any of this: civ1-science's `Player/added` rule hands each new player up to three random starting advances, and every `to.not.include` assertion in the file assumes a player who has discovered nothing. 98 tests, five consecutive clean runs.

Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan, completing what `registerRules.ts` started. Events bound to the singleton `Engine` and the event factories took their registries from singleton defaults, so a second game in the same process had no handlers of its own — its turn loop would never start.

Stage 4 of the engine serialisation plan. `static transient` declares the fields a class does not want saved, `allTransient()` collects them across the inheritance chain, and `stateKeys()` reports what would be saved.

Opt-out, not opt-in: a field added later is saved by default, so forgetting to declare one wastes bytes. The reverse loses data silently, and a save format that quietly drops a new field is worse than one carrying a few it did not need.

`allTransient()` walks the prototype chain because `static` members are inherited rather than merged — a subclass declaring its own `transient` *replaces* its parent's, so without the walk `Derived` would silently start saving `_id` and `_keys` again. There is a test for exactly that.

What belongs in `transient` is anything the loading game supplies rather than the file: registries, the engine, the generator. Stage 3 is what makes that a clean idea — every constructor already takes those as parameters and a `Game` holds them, so a transient field is not a hole in the save, it is a field with a different source. Caches belong there too, for a different reason: they are derived, so restoring one restores a stale answer.
`stateKeys()` is only possible at all because of Stage 1. With `#private` fields `Object.keys` returned nothing, so no generic serialiser could exist.

The list's own entry was wrong about the largest cause. It carried both packages through three stages as "shared registry state between tests, which Stage 3 per-Game registries make properly fixable". Two of the three real causes were that. The third, behind five of civ1-city's eight failures, was three dependencies declared as `github:` specs while `library-city` ranges on them — two copies of each package installed, so `instanceof` compared two distinct class objects. Registry threading would never have touched it, and the plan had a note putting a game-rules question to dom111 on the strength of the wrong diagnosis. That note is replaced with the actual cause and the one command that finds it.

Also fix the procedure's script order. It ran `ts:compile` before `prettier:format` so the generated `.d.ts` would not reformat in the diff, which is right, but it left every `.js.map` describing the *unformatted* source — formatting then rewrote that source out from under it. Stage 3 published 17 `registerRules.js.map` files in that state; the emitted `.js` was byte-identical, so nothing failed and the maps just pointed at the wrong lines. Now format, compile, format, with `script` separate from `label` because `hasScript` looks the label up in `package.json` and would have skipped the new step in silence.
The pattern that fixed city:captured does not finish the job, and the reason is worth stating precisely so nobody burns an afternoon on it.

cost.test.ts's three failures are a missing PopulationSupportFood yield, and the yield appears as soon as `workedTileRegistry` is threaded into `cityCreated` so worker assignment lands in the test's own registry. That breaks twelve currently-passing corruption tests in the same file, because their expected values were established while worker assignment went to the singleton — while the city under test effectively had no workers assigned.

So either those corruption expectations are right for a city with no assigned workers and the fixture should not assign any, or they were silently wrong and threading the registry through exposes it. That is a civ1 game-rules question, not a testing one, so it is written down rather than guessed at.
dom111 fixed `city:captured`, and the shape generalises.

These tests construct some registries and let the rest default to the module singletons, which are shared across every test file in the process. The fix is to construct all of them, pass them positionally with `undefined` for the slots the test does not care about, and — the part that is not mechanical — set up the state the rules actually require.

`captured` looks up a `PlayerWorld` for the capturing player and previously found one only because another test file had leaked it into the singleton. So each failure is really the question "what state was this rule finding by accident?", and the answer differs per rule.

This replaces the earlier note that called the fix intractable. It is not; it just is not a single mechanical pass, and a `Game` is the wrong tool because it changes which registry the rules and `setUpCity` each use.

Stages 2 and 3 were mechanical because the types already said what the answer was. `transient` is the same shape of problem: a field typed with a registry class, `Engine` or a generator is something the loading `Game` supplies, so it is transient by construction. Caches are the other category and are matched by name, because a cache has no distinguishing type.

Narrowed to what is actually saved, the codemod derives declarations for 29 `DataObject` classes across 24 packages with nothing left unclassifiable — and it agrees with the plan's own worked examples exactly, `Tile` and `City` included, which is the check that matters.
Three things it needed, each found by getting one wrong first:

Follow the inheritance chain across packages — `Unit extends Buildable extends DataObject` spans three, and without closing over the tree `SimpleAIClient`, a client rather than an entity, was handed a declaration for its arrow-function fields.
Read the initialiser when there is no annotation: `private _attributes = new AttributeRegistry()` says what it holds as clearly as a type would.
Exclude registries. Their membership is saved as id lists against the save's entity table, not as fields of the registry.
An attempt at civ1-city got partway and is worth writing down rather than repeating.

Passing a `Game` for every registry does remove the leakage those tests suffer from — `city:captured` failing with "Wrong number of player worlds" because the player worlds came from whatever test file ran before it. But it produces a different failure: the `Created` rules register and never fire, 7 of them in `game.rules`, a `City` built against that same registry, and `game.cities` still empty.

The tests were written against the split they were accidentally creating. The rule factory's own `ruleRegistry` parameter defaulted to the singleton while `setUpCity` processed `Created` against the test's registry — two registries, and the assertions depend on that. Making them one, which is correct, changes what the rules do.
So it needs the tests' intent re-established rule by rule, not a mechanical pass. Stopped rather than guess at assertions.
Three things the earlier stages changed about it, worth writing down before the context is lost.

The surface, measured: 53 classes carry private fields, 36 of those fields are registry- or `Engine`-typed and 133 are state. So `transient` is almost exactly "the registry-typed fields", and after Stage 1 they all have explicit types — which makes it type-directed like Stages 2 and 3, not 24 hand-written lists.

Stage 3 makes most of it moot at load time: a registry field needs neither saving nor rehydrating, because the loading `Game` has the registry and every constructor already takes it. `transient` becomes "fields the `Game` supplies", which is a better-defined idea, and it means the hydrator wants a `Game`.
One thing got worse: `toPlainObject` emits `Rule` internals at `Unit.busy`, and fixing it properly needs Stage 6's named rules.
Also records what widening the checksum costs — three stages of comparability — and that the two known-failing suites are the smallest demonstration that the `Game` context was worth building.

**Two games in one process, proven.** `npm run test:isolation` builds two `Game`s, registers the turn loop against each, and checks 13 ways that they share nothing: registries, rule registries, engines, turns, the civ1 registries, entities, events, turn state and random streams.

`civ publish` now decides npm-versus-GitHub by `publishConfig.access` rather than by the installed path alone. Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan. `registerRules.ts` registered into the module-level `RuleRegistry` at import time, and each rule factory was called with no arguments so it picked up its own singleton registries. `register(game)` passes the game's registries to each factory instead. Which slot each parameter wants is not a judgement: the factories are already fully typed with the registry classes they take, so it is a lookup, and the codemod reads the signatures rather than guessing.

Importing the module still registers into `defaultGame`. The plugin loader works by importing each package for that side effect, and `defaultGame` adopts the existing singletons, so this changes nothing for anyone who has not moved yet. Dropping it would produce a game with silently absent rules — no error, just wrong behaviour.

Stage 3 of the engine serialisation plan, and the piece that unlocks the rest of it: multiplayer, test isolation, and loading a save into a fresh context rather than mutating the running game.

`Game` holds the 43 registries plus turn, year and the random number generator. The dependency injection it needs already existed — every class and every rule factory in the engine takes its registries as constructor parameters with singleton defaults. What was missing was something to pass.

`defaultGame` adopts the existing singletons instead of constructing its own. That is deliberate and it is what makes the migration incremental: while some packages still import `instance` and others take a `Game`, both must see the same registry. Otherwise a half-migrated engine disagrees with itself, and that failure looks like a rule not firing rather than like an error.
Two departures from the plan's sketch, both forced:

It sketched `core-city` re-exporting `defaultGame.cities` as its `instance`, which would make every registry package depend on `core-game` — a cycle. Adoption runs the dependency the other way and needs no change to the registry packages at all.

It also implied every registry in the tree. `civ1-earth-generator`'s two are excluded: baking a specific ruleset into core is wrong, and it would drag `canvas` in with it. What remains is 43, which is the count 01-constraints.md reached independently.

A ruleset's own context — `civ1-game` — subclasses `Game` and adds its registries. Constructing it with only its own slots silently gives it *fresh* core registries rather than the adopted singletons, so it would disagree with every unmigrated package about what the city registry is.
`defaultSlots` makes the fix obvious at the call site: `new Game({ ...defaultSlots, ...mine })`.

`Engine` carries the event stream a game runs on — `turn:start`, `player:turn-end` and the rest. Two games sharing one would each see the other's turns start, which makes it per-game state as much as any registry.

It is also the last parameter type the rule factories take that had no slot: across the seventeen packages with a `registerRules.ts`, 86 factories take 25 distinct parameter types, and with this one every single one maps to a `Game` slot. That is what makes the migration mechanical rather than a judgement per factory.
Three separate problems, all in the tests.

`expect(spy).called` and `expect(spy).not.called` are property accesses, not assertions — chai-spies wants `to.have.been.called()`. Every spy expectation in this file was a no-op, which is why 'should respect `Strategy` `Priority`s' registered two identical `Strategy`s, asserted a specific one ran, and never once failed.

'should filter inactive `Strategy`s' tested `canHandle`, removed in b1888be 'Remove `canHandle` from `Strategy` and `Routine`'. Nothing filters anything now. Its only live assertion was that `attempt()` returns true while a bare `Strategy` — whose `attempt` throws by design — was in the registry, so it passed or failed on which one the random tie-break put first: three runs in eight. Removed; 'should stop calling `Strategy`s after the first successful `attempt()`' covers the real behaviour.

The two remaining ordering tests now set an actual `Priority` `Rule` instead of relying on the tie-break, so what they claim to test is what decides whether they pass. Verified by inverting an assertion and watching it fail — worth doing after finding a file's worth that could not.

As written it installs `github` from the registry — an unrelated, deprecated package, since renamed to `@octokit/rest` — on every install of this package.

localChanges: `tools/stage3.js` and `tools/codemod/register-game.js` move each of the seventeen `registerRules.ts` files from registering into module singletons at import time to `register(game)`. Which `Game` slot each factory parameter wants is read from the factory's own type signature rather than guessed: 133 factories across the seventeen, and every parameter type maps to a slot.
Two bugs in this repo's own tooling, both found by the conformance suite going silent rather than by anything failing:

`civ sync` preserved each package's `main` entrypoint — `buildPluginList` needs it to exist — but never refreshed it. Excluding a file from deletion is not the same as keeping it current. `node_modules` was serving a `core-game/index.js` from before `defaultSlots` was exported, so `defaultSlots` came back `undefined`, `civ1-game`'s `defaultGame` silently built its own registries instead of adopting the singletons, and `civ1-world`'s rules — including the one that builds the world — registered somewhere nothing would ever read. The game simply stopped after `engine:start` with no error at all. That is exactly the failure mode 05-engine-plan.md predicts for this stage, arriving by an unexpected route.

The codemod was not idempotent: re-run over an already-migrated file it found the new `game.rules.register(...)` call and rewrote its parent again, emitting `export const register = export const register = ...`. A rollout across seventeen packages gets re-run after any one of them fails, so it now detects its own output and skips.

Its compile and tests cannot run here at all: around twenty `github:` dependencies, each of which npm resolves with a nested install, recursively. Listed with the reason and reported on every publish, because a package there is released on strictly less evidence than the others and that should be visible rather than assumed.
It is also GitHub-resolved, so releasing it is a push and no tarball is built — and the change it carries touches only `package.json`, so there is no compiled output that could go stale.
`pnpm update` raised each declared range to the version it resolved. Every one stays within `^0.1.x`, so the version strategy in 04-package-workflow.md holds and no dependent needs widening.
The lockfile alongside is the record of which versions were verified together — the set the conformance suite last ran green against.

Stage 2 of the engine serialisation plan. Nineteen packages call `Math.random()`, so nothing about a game is reproducible: no replay testing, and a save/load cycle would change the next combat result.

Overriding `Math.random` globally at worker boot would fix that for one game and needs no engine change at all — but it cannot survive Stage 3, where two `Game`s in one process would share the override and interleave their draws. So the generator is injected instead, with this module's `instance` as the default everywhere, which is the pattern `core-spaceship` already used.

`calls()` is the part that is easy to leave out and expensive to add later. A save recording only the seed would restart the stream rather than resume it, so a game saved before a battle and reloaded would fight it differently. mulberry32 makes `restore(seed, calls)` O(1) rather than a replay, because its state after n draws is `seed + n * increment` (mod 2^32).

It is deliberately its own package rather than part of `core-rule`: four of the nineteen consumers do not depend on `core-rule`, and making them pull in the rule engine to get a random number would be the wrong trade.

localChanges: `core-game` exists and its acceptance criterion holds: two `Game`s in one process share no registries, turn, year or random stream. The 17 `registerRules.ts` migrations remain.

`resolutionOf` returned "npm" when a package was not installed. That is the dangerous default: it offers a package that lives only on GitHub to `npm publish` as a new private scoped package. It also meant a damaged `node_modules` produced a confidently wrong publish plan — sixteen packages listed as pending when two were.

`simple-ai-client` cannot be installed, and pointing its `node_modules/@civ-clone` at the renderer's looked like a way around that. npm prunes through such a symlink: a killed install in that checkout deleted 106 packages from web-renderer's `node_modules`, three of them direct dependencies.

pnpm does not repair it — `pnpm install`, even with `--force`, reports "Already up to date" from its state file without checking that the hoisted links still exist. Only `rm -rf node_modules && pnpm install` brings it back.

Four packages carry a `ts-mocha ./tests/*.test.ts` script from a template and have never had a `tests/` directory. The gate reported them as "ts-mocha is not installed", which reads like lost coverage; there is none to lose.
The checksums did not move: 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b, as before Stage 1, and seed 2 still gives what it gave before any of this started.
Also records the three pre-existing broken suites this stage ran into, each verified to fail identically at the commit before the change, and why `core-strategy`'s cannot be fixed by choosing a seed.
Both found by verifying against the registry rather than trusting the tool's own "published" line.

`--pending` deliberately operates on packages the manifest no longer lists — a stage drops them once its work is done — so `manifest.packages[name]` was `undefined` and `resolution` with it. That read as "not github", and `simple-world-generator`, which has never been on npm and is consumed straight from its default branch, was offered to `npm publish` as a new scoped package. npm refused with E402 because scoped packages default to restricted; on an account with a paid plan it would have quietly created a private package. Resolution now comes from the installed tree, which cannot go stale that way.
The second is subtler. npm has two near-identically worded conflicts:
Cannot publish over the previously published versions   — already done Cannot publish over previously staged version           — did NOT finish

Matching loosely on "cannot publish over" treated the second as success, so `core-civ-client@0.1.2` was reported published, tagged and pushed while the registry had only 0.1.1. It finalised on its own a few minutes later, but the tool had already moved on and would not have retried. Staged now raises, saying what it means and that a re-run is safe.

`civ1-city-improvement`'s suite fails 2-3 tests per run, and 6 before Stage 2 touched it — RNG-dependent build-availability assertions, and `WorkedTileRegistry` singleton state leaking between tests. Neither is Stage 2's to fix, and refusing on them means the package can never ship again.

It is recorded in the gate with its reason rather than passed as a flag, so it is visible in review and hard to forget. The suite still runs and the failure is still reported — as a skip, never as a pass — and nothing goes on the list without first checking it fails identically at the commit before the change.

The manifest reports work *remaining*, so when a stage's codemod lands its packages drop out of that stage's set — taking the wave mapping with them and leaving `civ publish --wave N --stage 2` with nothing to publish. That is correct as a description of remaining work and useless as a publish plan, and it bit once per stage.

`--pending` asks the checkouts instead: anything with commits its remote does not have, a version the registry does not have, or no upstream at all (a package a stage introduced). It orders them into waves from the live dependency graph, so `core-random` publishes before the eighteen packages that now depend on it without anyone maintaining a list.

The conformance harness now seeds `@civ-clone/core-random`'s instance instead of overriding `Math.random` globally. The override worked, but it could not survive Stage 3 — two `Game`s in one process would share it — and it could only ever prove the *harness* was deterministic, not that the engine had stopped using the global.

So `Math.random` is instrumented rather than replaced: every call is counted and the count goes in the snapshot, where a non-zero value is a visible failure. It reads 0 at turns 1, 10 and 50. Grepping the source cannot show that, because it cannot see what a dependency resolves to at runtime.

The count sits outside the checksum, alongside the DTO digest, for the same reason: the checksum answers "is the engine state the same", and adding an instrument should not change the number it exists to watch. It did on the first run, which is how the boundary got drawn.

With that, Stage 2 leaves every checksum identical — 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b, as before Stage 1 — and seed 2 still produces the same three checksums it produced before any of this started. Nineteen packages moved off `Math.random` and the draw sequence did not shift.

Tooling: `tools/lib/procedure.js` extracts the per-package procedure the stage drivers share; `tools/stage2.js` and `tools/codemod/seeded-rng.js` drive this stage; `civ audit` now computes publish waves per stage, because computing them once over the stage 1 set left every stage 2 package with no wave at all once stage 1 landed.

All 62 packages are published and pushed. A clean reinstall resolves every one at its new version, with zero drift in the 263 packages Stage 1 never touched, and the conformance checksums are unchanged against the published artifacts — 7d6b6b04 / 73a0cc05 / 3431063b, as before.
Committing the lockfile because it is now the record of which versions were verified together, which is what 04-package-workflow.md asks for and what a bisect would need.
`pnpm-workspace.yaml` carries the settings that make `pnpm install` work at all on pnpm 11, each earned from a failure:
`overrides` restored from the lockfile, which recorded pins no config declared any more (ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH)
`blockExoticSubdeps: false`, because 22 of these packages are `github:` declared and depend on each other that way (ERR_PNPM_EXOTIC_SUBDEP)

`minimumReleaseAge: 0`, because pnpm 11 refuses very recently published versions and ours were minutes old. This one failed silently: resolution quietly chose the previous version of all 62 while the registry had the new ones, so a conformance run would have tested the old code and passed.
`allowBuilds` filled in, replacing the placeholders pnpm wrote itself
`glob` moves into devDependencies: `buildPluginList.js` has always required it without declaring it, and was resolving through hoisting that a clean install no longer provides.

localChanges: Wave 0 published `core-registry@0.1.2` successfully, and then every way of checking said it had not: `npm view` and the registry's package document are both served from a cache that can lag minutes behind a publish. The only straight answer came from trying to publish again, which said "cannot publish over the previously published versions".

So the pre-check now asks for the exact version rather than the version list — the least stale answer available — and is treated as a hint rather than proof. The conflict itself is read as success, because a stale "not published" on the fourth of twenty packages would otherwise abort the wave half-done.

The first real publish stopped at npm's `EOTP`: this account has two-factor authentication on writes. `npm version patch` had already run, so `core-registry` was left with a local `0.1.2` commit and tag, unpublished and unpushed — recoverable, but only because nothing had been pushed yet.
A retry would have bumped it again, skipping `0.1.2` and leaving that tag pointing at something never published. So `release` is now idempotent:
the tag `npm version` writes is the record that the bump has happened, so a version already bumped is not bumped again
a version already on the registry is not republished

`--otp CODE` passes a 2FA code through. One code covers one publish before its thirty-second window closes, so a wave of twenty needs either an automation token or 2FA set to authorisation-only; `civ publish` says so rather than failing part-way through a wave.
`--dry-run` now reads the live checkout rather than the recorded manifest version, so it cannot claim a package is about to move to the version it is already on.
All twelve waves pass `civ publish --wave N --dry-run`; verify-stage1 reports 0 of 62 needing attention. Nothing is published or pushed.
Also records two findings from getting there:

`core-city`'s suite had been failing deterministically since 2022 — it asserted a city works one tile, when nothing in that package creates a `WorkedTile`, so it was reading whatever the shared registry singleton happened to hold. Fixed in core-city's own `test:` commit.

The first attempt at that fix appeared to do nothing, because a committed `tests/lib/setUpCity.js` sat beside the edited `.ts` and ts-node resolves the `.js`. Same trap as 04-package-workflow.md §1, one level down, and worth stating plainly: a compiled file beside edited source is the first explanation to reach for when an edit seems to have no effect.
Six ways the gate refused a package that was fine, all found by dry-running all twelve waves before publishing anything:

Untracked files counted as a dirty tree. Every untracked file in this tree is a lockfile; npm never packs `package-lock.json`, and the packages carrying a stray `pnpm-lock.yaml` are all GitHub-resolved and so produce no tarball. They are now reported beside the result instead of refused.

A forced rebuild always changes the tree, because the committed `.js` are single-quoted, current `tsc` emits double, and `prettier:format` globs only `**/*.ts` so it never reformats them. "Did the tree change" cannot tell that from genuine staleness. The gate now tests for what staleness actually looks like — compiled output still carrying TypeScript's private-field WeakMap helpers — and reports the reformatting as a note.

The compile was not forced, so `tsc --build` skipped whenever its outputs were newer than its inputs. A skipped compile is indistinguishable from a successful one, which is how five packages came to hold compiled output that had never matched their source.
`core-strategy`'s suite is flaky by construction and failed the gate on a coin flip. It now retries before refusing.

Five packages declare a `ts-mocha` test script without listing `ts-mocha` in devDependencies, so their suites have never been runnable. A missing runner is now detected by looking for the binary rather than by reading an error, and reported as a skip — never as a pass.
`simple-ai-client` cannot be installed at all (its ~20 `github:` dependencies each spawn a nested install, recursively), so it falls back to the renderer's own tsc and prettier.
The checks also restore the checkout when they finish, so `npm publish` packs what the commit and the tag hold rather than the output of the check that just ran.
Stage 0 of docs/engine-serialisation/05-engine-plan.md, plus everything Stage 1 needed in order to be provable.

tools/civ — audit, clone, sync, watch, collisions, check-dts, publish. `audit` recomputes the whole picture from node_modules rather than trusting a hand-maintained list, and reproduces 04-package-workflow.md's table exactly: 325 installed, 22 resolved from GitHub, 62 packages carrying 282 `#private` declarations across 12 publish waves, 17 `registerRules.ts`, 19 packages calling `Math.random`, one three-package dependency cycle.
tools/codemod/private-fields.js — the ts-morph codemod. It also walks class expressions, because `getClasses()` returns declarations only and `core-unit-transport` builds its `Transport` as a mixin.
tools/stage1.js — the per-package procedure. It records what was already failing before it touches anything, so a package that never compiled is reported rather than blamed on the change.
tools/verify-stage1.js — the sweep that catches a commit whose `.js` predates its `.ts`, which is what a silently skipped compile leaves behind.

tests/engine/ — the conformance suite. A seeded four-player game to turn 50 in 11 seconds, recording engine state checksums and, separately, the size and hash of what `toPlainObject()` emits. Separately because Stage 1 leaves the first identical and moves the second; see fixtures/NOTES.md.
tests/engine/hydration.ts — `Object.assign(Object.create(City.prototype), state).name()` returning a value. The point of the whole stage.

Both bundle with esbuild rather than running under ts-node: node resolution finds each package's compiled `.js` first, so a plain require would test the published artifact instead of the source `civ sync` just wrote.

localChanges:
The moment when, after many years

of hard work and a long voyage

you stand in the centre of your room,

house, half-acre, square mile, island, country,

knowing at last how you got there,

and say, I own this,

        

is the same moment when the trees unloose

their soft arms from around you,

the birds take back their language,

the cliffs fissure and collapse,

the air moves back from you like a wave

and you can't breathe.



No, they whisper. You own nothing.

You were a visitor, time after time

climbing the hill, planting the flag, proclaiming.

We never belonged to you.

You never found us.

It was always the other way round.
